background: Bowen Baker studied at MIT, earning a B.S. and an M.Eng. in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. His first machine-learning work was on automated neural architecture search at the MIT Media Lab: MetaQNN, which used reinforcement learning to design convolutional network architectures, and his master's thesis 'Towards Practical Neural Network Meta-Modeling', which received an award. He has said he has always been interested in self-improving systems, which he saw as a core requirement for AGI-like systems.

He joined OpenAI in December 2017, first on the robotics team, where he contributed to sim-to-real transfer and dexterous in-hand manipulation with a robotic hand ('Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation', 2018). In September 2018 he moved to the Multi-Agent team with Igor Mordatch and led 'Emergent Tool Use from Multi-Agent Autocurricula' (ICLR 2020), the hide-and-seek experiments in which agents discovered six successive strategies, including using boxes and ramps as tools and exploiting the physics engine ('box surfing'). He later led Video PreTraining (VPT, 2022), which learned behavioural priors for Minecraft from unlabelled online video, and co-authored 'Let's Verify Step by Step' (2023) on process supervision for LLM reasoning.

Around 2023 he shifted to AI safety and alignment. He led 'Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation' (March 2025), which showed that a weaker model (GPT-4o) monitoring the chain-of-thought of a frontier reasoning model can detect reward hacking far better than monitoring actions alone, but that penalising 'bad thoughts' causes models to hide their intent. He was a co-author of the cross-lab position paper 'Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety' (2025). As of 2026 he leads OpenAI's Chain-of-Thought Interpretability team and speaks widely on preserving CoT monitorability.

background: Bronson Schoen is an AI alignment researcher at Apollo Research with a background in software engineering; his LinkedIn lists about 12 years of professional experience. Before moving into AI safety he was a senior software engineer at NVIDIA working on autonomous vehicles (April 2022–September 2024). Details of his education were not found in public sources.

He joined Apollo Research in September 2024 as a senior research engineer on AI evaluations (later member of technical staff), working on scheming—AI systems covertly pursuing misaligned goals. He was an equal-contribution first author, with Alexander Meinke and Jérémy Scheurer, of 'Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming' (December 2024), which found that several frontier models could engage in scheming behaviours such as disabling oversight, attempting self-exfiltration and sandbagging when given goals in context.

He was lead author of 'Stress Testing Deliberative Alignment for Anti-Scheming Training' (September 2025), a joint Apollo Research–OpenAI study that used 'covert actions' as a proxy for scheming and found deliberative alignment training reduced covert action rates sharply (e.g. OpenAI o3 from 13% to 0.4%) but did not eliminate them, with results complicated by models' growing awareness that they were being evaluated. He co-authored Apollo/OpenAI's 'Measuring Reward-Seeking via Contrastive Belief Updates' (2026). In an August 2026 Cognitive Revolution podcast episode he discussed his work reading unfiltered reasoning traces from frontier-lab RL training, describing metagaming, reward seeking and motivated chain-of-thought reasoning.

bronson-schoen.views: Schoen's work holds that highly capable AI systems could secretly pursue misaligned goals and that, because a scheming AI would deliberately hide this, assessing anti-scheming interventions requires testing far out-of-distribution, checking whether good behaviour is driven by evaluation awareness, and testing robustness to pre-existing misaligned goals. He has emphasised that RL training can produce metagaming and reward-seeking visible in raw reasoning traces. No numeric timelines found.

background: Catherine Olsson grew up in the Seattle area (Lakeside School, 2008) and studied at MIT (2008–2013), double-majoring in computer science and brain and cognitive science, with research at the MIT Media Lab and MIT CSAIL. She began a computational neuroscience PhD at New York University (2013–2016), leaving with a master's degree; during this period she contributed to the Open Science Collaboration's landmark 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science' (Science, 2015).

She joined OpenAI as a software engineer (2016–2017), where she built the REST API for OpenAI Gym, and then worked as a research software engineer at Google Brain (2017–2019) on Ian Goodfellow's team, working on GANs and adversarial examples, including 'Skill Rating for Generative Models' and 'Unrestricted Adversarial Examples', and contributing to the CleverHans library. In 2018 she appeared on the 80,000 Hours Podcast with Daniel Ziegler advising people on fast paths into AI safety engineering. From 2019 to 2021 she was a Senior Program Associate at Open Philanthropy, funding technical research on potential risks from advanced AI.

In March 2021 she joined Anthropic as an early member of technical staff. She worked on the mechanistic interpretability team led by Chris Olah and was first author of 'In-context Learning and Induction Heads' (2022), which identified induction-head circuits as a mechanism behind in-context learning in transformers. She also co-authored 'A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits' (2021), 'Toy Models of Superposition' (2022), 'Training a Helpful and Harmless Assistant with RLHF' (2022), 'Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms' (2022), 'Constitutional AI' (2022) and 'Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations' (2022). She remains at Anthropic as of 2026.

She has advocated that people interested in AI safety 'just dive in' to ML engineering rather than waiting for a PhD. No numeric timelines or p(doom) found.

background: Charlie O'Neill is an Australian machine-learning researcher and founder. He studied at the Australian National University as a Tuckwell Scholar, earning a Bachelor of Science (major in Mathematical Modelling, minors in Applied Statistics and Computer Science) and a Bachelor of Economics. From 2020 to 2023 he worked as a machine-learning researcher at Macuject, and he co-founded Rake News, a platform for personalised, debiased news using language models.

As a 2025 General Sir John Monash Scholar he began a DPhil in machine learning at the University of Oxford under Jakob Foerster, but left to build companies. He co-founded Parsed, serving as CTO, to build specialised open-source models intended to beat frontier labs on specific tasks; Parsed raised a seed round and was acquired by the inference company Baseten at the end of 2025. At Baseten he became a research scientist (December 2025) and then Head / Co-Head of Model Training (2026), running the team that trained bespoke models for individual customers.

As of 2026 he runs Base Labs, a research lab within Baseten that aims to 'advance and democratise open-source intelligence' by studying how models learn, remember, specialise and get cheaper to run, and publishing open environments, data, recipes and models—including failures. In September 2026 he joined John Schulman and Beren Millidge on a Dwarkesh Patel panel, 'AI researchers debate how close we are to recursive self-improvement', where he discussed post-training team structure, distillation and RL environment design.

charlie-oneill.views: On the Dwarkesh panel O'Neill argued that recursive self-improvement may be a 'cumulative task'—innovations like attention, mixture-of-experts and GRPO can be stacked once discovered—whereas much real-world work (e.g. legal work) is messy and non-stationary, which leads to 'perhaps unintuitive predictions such as why RSI might land before continual learning (and why it's going to be hard to get off the current paradigm even if it's wrong)'. He expects drop-in remote workers relatively soon but is more cautious about large research uplift, citing humans' capacity to absorb information and choose the next experiment as a bottleneck, and he described automating AI research as roughly 'ASI-complete' because some tasks need far more than today's context windows.

background: Christina Smith Montgomery (March 21, 1870 – August 27, 1965) was a Scottish born Australian headmistress. She was the founding head of Melbourne Girls' High School which became the Mac.Robertson Girls' High School.

p: Montgomery was born in Kelso in the Scottish Borders where she gained a love for classical studies at Kelso Grammar School. When she was a teenager, her parents William and Janet (born Smith) emigrated. Christina and her sister, Margaret, renewed their education in Melbourne at Cambridge Street State School where they became pupil-teachers. Together they studied at Melbourne Teachers' College from 1891 where they both won prizes. Christina went on to the University of Melbourne where she graduated in 1897.  She gained a Master's degree in 1900. Victoria's Department of Education had appointed its first director, Frank Tate, and it had begun to employ women graduates. Montgomery was one of the first.

Tate noticed the Junior teacher, Montgomery, had respect from her classes despite her small size, but she had to wait to find promotion. She went to work for Perth Central Girls' School for a year and when she returned she was promoted. In 1905 she was teaching Latin at Melbourne Continuation School. In 1923 she became the headmistress under the head of the, then, co-educational school. The school was split into two halves in 1927. The boys moved to create Melbourne Boys' High School in South Yarra. The remaining building was condemned but the girls continued to be educated there. It was renamed Melbourne Girls' High School and Montgomery was its headmistrss.

In 1930 the school was moved to Government House. When she retired in 1932 it was said that she still at her height of her career. There were over 800 students in the school paying six pounds every term. Five years before there had been less than four hundred. There was a ceremony at the Lyceum Club in Melbourne with 50 fellow teachers present.

background: Rev. Daniel Ziegler (June 11, 1804 Reading, Pennsylvania – May 23, 1876 York, Pennsylvania) was a minister in Kreutz Creek and York, Pennsylvania, and also an avid entomologist. He was a friend of Dr. Frederick Ernst Melsheimer (1782–1873), who like his father the Rev. Frederick Valentine Melsheimer (1749–1814), was also a keen entomologist. Their collections ended up in Harvard University's Museum of Comparative Zoology, and comprised 14,774 specimens from 5,302 different species.

Ziegler studied at the University of Pennsylvania and, later, theology at the German Reformed Seminary in York. He was the minister for 37 years of Kraeutz-Creek Church near York as well as up to eight other churches. With his wife, Eve Eyster, he had 10 children, including son Dr. H. A. Ziegler.

It was during his time as minister at Kraeutz-Creek that he began studying entomology. He often accompanied his father on insect-collecting excursions, using the beat net method of collecting, uncommon in America at the time.
Rev. Ziegler's only entomological paper, a description of 36 new species of Coleoptera, was published for the assistance of Dr. Melsheimer, whose home was close to one of Rev. Ziegler's churches.
There was nothing whatever eventful in his life, and besides his few entomological contributions, he was nothing more than a plain, plodding, honest country parson.

Gregory Brockman (born November 29, 1987) is an American entrepreneur and software engineer. He is co-founder and president of OpenAI. He began his career at Stripe in 2010, upon leaving MIT, and became CTO in 2013. He left Stripe in 2015 to co-found OpenAI, where he also served as CTO.

p: Brockman was born in Thompson, North Dakota, and attended Red River High School, where he excelled in mathematics, chemistry, and computer science. He won a silver medal in the 2006 International Chemistry Olympiad and became the first finalist from North Dakota to participate in the Intel science talent search since 1973. In 2003, 2005, and 2007, he attended Canada/USA Mathcamp, a summer program for mathematically talented high-school students. In 2008, Brockman enrolled at Harvard University but left a year later, briefly enrolling at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

In 2010, he dropped out of MIT to join Stripe, a company founded by Patrick Collison, his MIT classmate, and John Collison. In 2013, he became Stripe's first CTO, while the company grew from 5 to 205 employees. Brockman left Stripe in May 2015.

Brockman met with Sam Altman and Elon Musk, and led the recruiting of the OpenAI founding team. Many of its members, including Ilya Sutskever, were top AI research talent that left high paying jobs for the opportunity at OpenAI. He co-founded OpenAI in December 2015 alongside Altman, Sutskever and others. The company initially operated from Brockman's living room.
He led various projects at OpenAI, including OpenAI Gym and OpenAI Five, a Dota 2 bot.

On February 14, 2019, OpenAI announced that they had developed a new large language model called GPT-2, but kept it private due to their concern for its potential misuse. They released the model to a limited group of beta testers in May 2019.

In November 2019 after a year of dating, Brockman married Anna at OpenAI's offices on a workday. Ilya Sutskever officiated the wedding. As of July 2026, Brockman's net worth was estimated at $25.5 billion according to Bloomberg Billionaires Index, with the vast majority of his fortune coming from his stake in OpenAI.

background: Gus Docker is a Danish podcast host who studied philosophy and computer science at the University of Copenhagen. He has been active in Effective Altruism Denmark and previously hosted the Utilitarian podcast, interviewing philosophers and researchers on ethics and effective altruism.

In 2022 he took over as host of the Future of Life Institute (FLI) Podcast from Lucas Perry; his first episodes as 'the new host' in October 2022 covered nuclear command, control and communications with Philip Reiner and nuclear winter with Brian Toon, and soon afterwards he interviewed Ajeya Cotra on forecasting transformative AI. He is FLI's Podcast Host & Director and part of its core team and communications group, overseeing production of the show, which features conversations with researchers, policy experts, philosophers and technologists on the risks and opportunities of AI, biotechnology and nuclear weapons.

Under his hosting the podcast has featured a large number of AI safety, alignment and governance researchers and advocates—for example Epoch AI's Ege Erdil on the GATE model and AGI timelines (2025), ControlAI's Andrea Miotti and the AI Whistleblower Initiative's Karl Koch—as well as episodes on AI companions, AI policy and existential hope. As of 2026 he continues to host and direct the FLI Podcast.

As FLI's host he frames AI as a source of potential extreme large-scale risk. No personal numeric forecasts found.

background: Hannah Mary Fry (born 21 February 1984) is an English mathematician, author and broadcaster. She is the first Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge, and a fellow of Queens' College, Cambridge. She was previously the president of the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications and was a professor of the mathematics of cities at University College London.

Her work has included studies of patterns of human behaviour, the mathematics behind pandemics, and scientific explanations of modern appliances. She has had a particular focus on helping the public to improve their mathematical skills. Fry gave the Royal Institution Christmas Lectures in 2019 and has presented several television and radio programmes for the BBC, including The Secret Genius of Modern Life. She has received several awards for her work in mathematics, including the Asimov Prize and David Attenborough Award.

p: Hannah Mary Fry was born in Harlow, Essex, England, on 21 February 1984. The middle of three sisters, she grew up in Hoddesdon and Ware, Hertfordshire. She is of English and Irish heritage: her father was an English factory worker making hydraulic lifts for lorries and her Irish Catholic mother stayed at home. One summer when she was around 11, her mother made her solve a page of problems in a mathematics textbook each day of the holiday, putting her ahead of other pupils when she went back to school. She attended Presdales School in Ware, where a teacher inspired her to study mathematics. She graduated from University College London (UCL) with a degree in mathematics. In 2011, she completed her thesis under the supervision of Frank T. Smith and was awarded a PhD from UCL for research on fluid dynamics and the Navier–Stokes equations.

Fry was appointed as a lecturer at University College London in 2012, working at the UCL Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis. She was later appointed senior lecturer, then professor in the Mathematics of Cities. In September 2022, she was elected a Fellow of the Royal Academy of Engineering. In 2024, she became president of the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications. She joined the Faculty of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge in January 2025 as the university's first Professor of the Public Understanding of Mathematics.

Fry has attempted to overturn the stereotype that mathematics is "boring" and not worth studying. Although she acknowledges the subject is difficult, she believes it is possible to frame it in a manner that people can identify with.

2018: Christopher Zeeman Medal from the Institute of Mathematics and its Applications (IMA) and the London Mathematical Society "for her contributions to the public understanding of the mathematical sciences".
2020: Asimov Prize, a literary-scientific award organised by the Italian INFN Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare and GSSI graduate school Gran Sasso Science Institute, for Hello World.
2020: Honorary Fellowship of the Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET) on the 150th anniversary of the institution.
Fry lives in Greenwich, South London. She co-parents two daughters with her ex-husband. She has the quantum computer prop from the TV series Devs and uses it as a chandelier in her home.

In 2020, she was diagnosed with cervical cancer and underwent a radical hysterectomy. She wrote and presented the documentary Making Sense of Cancer with Hannah Fry for BBC Two's Horizon about her treatment and its long-term effects (which included lymphoedema, a chronic swelling condition). The film explores the statistics around disease screening and decision-making by patients and doctors. Fry subsequently had lymphaticovenular anastomosis, a reconstructive surgery. She later wrote of the cancer treatment "we took a very risk-averse route that we didn't need to", and that she regretted she could not have a third child.

background: Jerry Wei began research while still a student, working as a research assistant at Dartmouth College (2019–2021) with Saeed Hassanpour on deep learning for medical image analysis, including generative data augmentation and curriculum learning for digital pathology. He enrolled at Stanford University in 2021 to study computer science (AI track) and interned as a software engineer at Meta in 2022.

In November 2022 he joined Google Brain as a student researcher working on LLM reasoning with Quoc Le's team, producing 'Larger Language Models Do In-Context Learning Differently' (2023) and 'Symbol Tuning Improves In-Context Learning in Language Models' (2023). In July 2023 he left Stanford without finishing his degree to join Google DeepMind full-time as a research engineer on Gemini post-training, pivoting toward alignment with 'Simple Synthetic Data Reduces Sycophancy in Large Language Models' (2023) and 'Long-form Factuality in Large Language Models' (NeurIPS 2024), which introduced the LongFact benchmark and SAFE evaluator; he also co-authored FreshLLMs.

In mid-2024 he joined Anthropic (Alignment Science, then the Safeguards Research Team formed in 2025). He was a core author of 'Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming' (2025), which trains input/output classifiers from a natural-language constitution to block requests for dangerous information such as CBRN weapons, and of 'Constitutional Classifiers++: Efficient Production-Grade Defenses against Universal Jailbreaks' (2026). As of 2026 he leads Anthropic's deployment-robustness team, building production safety systems that defend Claude from misuse.

background: Lester Lawrence "Larry" Lessig III (born June 3, 1961) is an American legal scholar and political activist. He is the Roy L. Furman Professor of Law at Harvard Law School and the former director of the Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics at Harvard University. He is the founder of Creative Commons and Equal Citizens. Lessig was a candidate for the Democratic Party's nomination for president of the United States in the 2016 U.S. presidential election but withdrew before the primaries.

p: Lessig was born on June 3, 1961, in Rapid City, South Dakota, to Lester Lawrence "Jack" Lessig II (1929–2020) who was an engineer and Patricia "Pat" West Lessig (1930–2019), a real estate agent. He has two older step-siblings, Robert (died 2019) and Kitty, and a younger biological sister, Leslie. He grew up in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. He graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1983 with a double degree B.A. in economics and a B.S. in management. He then studied philosophy at Trinity College, Cambridge, receiving a M.A. in 1986. Lessig then returned to the United States to attend law school. He did his first year at the University of Chicago Law School before transferring to Yale Law School, and graduated in 1989 with a J.D. degree.

After graduation from law school, Lessig was a law clerk for Judge Richard Posner of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit from 1989 to 1990, and then for Justice Antonin Scalia of the U.S. Supreme Court from 1990 to 1991. Lessig started his academic career at the University of Chicago Law School, where he was professor from 1991 to 1997. As co-director of its Center for the Study of Constitutionalism in Eastern Europe, he helped the newly independent Republic of Georgia draft a constitution. From 1997 to 2000, he was at Harvard Law School, holding for a year the chair of Berkman Professor of Law, affiliated with the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. He subsequently joined Stanford Law School, where he established the Stanford Center for Internet and Society.

Lessig returned to Harvard in July 2009 as professor and director of the Edmond J. Safra Center for Ethics. In 2013, Lessig was appointed as the Roy L. Furman Professor of Law and Leadership at Harvard; his chair lecture was entitled "Aaron's Laws: Law

Lessig is a proponent of reduced legal restrictions on copyright, trademark, and radio frequency spectrum, particularly in technology applications. In 2001, he founded Creative Commons, a nonprofit organization devoted to expanding the range of creative works available for others to build upon and to share legally. Prior to his most recent appointment at Harvard, he was a professor of law at Stanford Law School, where he founded the Stanford Center for Internet and Society, and at the University of Chicago. He is a former board member of the Free Software Foundation and Software Freedom Law Center; the Washington, D.C. lobbying groups Public Knowledge and Free Press; and the Electronic Frontier Foundation. He was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 2007.

As a political activist, Lessig called for state-based activism to promote substantive reform of government with a Second Constitutional Convention. In May 2014, he launched a crowd-funded political action committee that he entitled Mayday PAC, with the purpose of electing candidates to Congress who would pass campaign finance reform. Lessig is also the co-founder of Rootstrikers, and is on the boards of MapLight and Represent.Us. He serves on the advisory boards of the Democracy Café, as well as the Sunlight Foundation.

In August 2015, Lessig announced that he was exploring a possible candidacy for president of the United States, promising to run if his exploratory committee raised $1 million by Labor Day. After accomplishing this, on September 6, 2015, Lessig announced that he was entering the race to become a candidate for the 2016 Democratic Party presidential nomination. Lessig described his candidacy as a referendum on campaign finance reform and electoral reform legislation. He stated that, if electe

Lessig came out in favor of a "right to warn" proposed by former OpenAI employees that would protect their right to warn the public of the catastrophic risks of AI. Lessig also agreed to work pro bono in defense of the whistleblowers. In August 2024, Lessig co-authored a letter alongside AI researchers Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, and Stuart Russell in favor of SB 1047, a California AI safety bill that would require companies training the most powerful models to perform risk assessments on their models before release. The letter argued that the bill would be a first step towards mitigating the severe risks posed by AI, and "the bare minimum for effective regulation of this technology". Lessig said that Gavin Newsom, the Governor of California, would have the opportunity to "cement California as a national first-mover in regulating AI".

In 2002, Lessig received the Award for the Advancement of Free Software from the Free Software Foundation (FSF). He also received the Scientific American 50 Award for having "argued against interpretations of copyright that could stifle innovation and discourse online." In 2006, Lessig was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

In 2011, Lessig was named to the Fastcase 50, "honoring the law's smartest, most courageous innovators, techies, visionaries, and leaders". Lessig was awarded honorary doctorates by the Faculty of Social Sciences at Lund University, Sweden in 2013 and by the Université catholique de Louvain in 2014. Lessig received the 2014 Webby Lifetime Achievement award for co-founding Creative Commons and defending net neutrality and the free and open software movement.

In May 2005, it was revealed that Lessig had experienced sexual abuse by the director at the American Boychoir School, which he had attended as an adolescent. Lessig reached a settlement with the school in the past, under confidential terms. He revealed his experiences in the course of representing another student victim, John Hardwicke, in court. In August 2006, he succeeded in persuading the New Jersey Supreme Court to radically restrict the scope of immunity,  which had protected nonprofits that failed to prevent sexual abuse from legal liability.
Lessig is married to Bettina Neuefeind, a German-born Harvard University colleague. The two married in 1999. He and Neuefeind have three children: Willem, Coffy, and Tess.

sections.h: Defamation lawsuit against The New York Times
p: In 2019, during the criminal investigation of Jeffrey Epstein, it was discovered that the MIT Media Lab under former director Joichi Ito had accepted secret donations from Epstein after Epstein had been convicted on criminal charges. Ito eventually resigned as director of the MIT Media Lab following this discovery. After making supportive comments to Ito, Lessig wrote a Medium post in September 2019 to explain his stance. In his post, Lessig acknowledged that universities should not take donations from convicted criminals such as Epstein who had become wealthy through actions unrelated to their criminal convictions; however, if such donations were to be accepted, it was better to take them secretly rather than publicly connect the university to the criminal.

Lessig's essay drew criticism, and about a week later Nellie Bowles of The New York Times had an interview with Lessig in which he reiterated his stance related to such donations broadly. The article used the headline "A Harvard Professor Doubles Down: If You Take Epstein's Money, Do It in Secret", which Lessig confirmed was based on a statement he had made to the Times. Lessig took issue with the headline overlooking his argument that MIT should not accept such donations in the first place and also criticized the first two lines of the article which read, "It is hard to defend soliciting donations from the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. But Lawrence Lessig, a Harvard Law professor, has been trying." He subsequently accused the Times of writing clickbait with the headline crafted to defame him, and stated that the circulation of the article on social media had hurt his reputation.
In January 2020, Lessig filed a defamation lawsuit against the Times, including writer Bowles, business editor Ellen Pollock, an

awards: FSF Award for the Advancement of Free Software (2003)

background: Leo Gao (online handle nabla_theta / bmk) rose to prominence in the open-source AI community. In July 2020 he co-founded EleutherAI with Connor Leahy and Sid Black, a decentralised research collective that began as a Discord server discussing GPT-3. He led the creation of The Pile (2020), an 825 GiB dataset of 22 diverse text sources for training large language models, and was central to the GPT-Neo project and the LM Evaluation Harness for standardised few-shot evaluation; he also contributed to GPT-NeoX-20B, BLOOM and BIG-bench. His 2020–2021 blog posts 'Building AGI Using Language Models' and 'Thoughts on the Alignment Implications of Scaling Language Models' argued that the world model embedded in large language models might be harnessed to build proto-AGI and explored what scaling meant for alignment.

He joined OpenAI in 2021 and has worked on alignment research there for over four years. He was lead author of 'Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization' (2022, with John Schulman and Jacob Hilton), co-authored the GPT-4 technical report and 'Weak-to-Strong Generalization' (2023), and led 'Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders' (2024), which trained sparse autoencoders with millions of latents on GPT-4. He co-authored 'Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation' (2025) and led work on interpretability via weight-sparse transformers ('circuit sparsity', 2025).

As of 2026 he describes himself as 'working on AGI alignment' at OpenAI. In talks he argues for an 'ambitious vision for interpretability'—aiming to fully understand neural networks rather than settling for partial explanations—and he has written an essay, 'An Alien Mind', on the state of AI and his concerns about the next few years.

leo-gao.views: Gao has expressed serious concern about AI risk, posting (as quoted on LessWrong): 'i've been at openai for 5 years. i think ai might kill everyone and we need to slow down.' He has written that he is concerned about the next few years and about the choices needed 'to keep the future in humanity's hands'. Technically, he argues interpretability should pursue the ambitious goal of fully understanding neural networks. Back in 2020 he argued that large language models' world models could be a route to proto-AGI. No explicit dated AGI forecast or p(doom) number was found.

background: Margaret Munnerlyn Mitchell (November 8, 1900 – August 16, 1949) was an American novelist and journalist. Mitchell wrote only one novel that was published during her lifetime, the American Civil War-era novel Gone with the Wind, for which she won the National Book Award for Fiction for Most Distinguished Novel of 1936 and the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1937. Long after her death, a collection of Mitchell's girlhood writings and a novella she wrote as a teenager, titled Lost Laysen, were published. A collection of newspaper articles written by Mitchell for The Atlanta Journal was republished in book form.

p: While the Great War carried on in Europe (1914–1918), Margaret Mitchell attended Atlanta's Washington Seminary (now The Westminster Schools), a "fashionable" private girls' school with an enrollment of over 300 students. She was very active in the Drama Club. Mitchell played the male characters: Nick Bottom in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream and Launcelot Gobbo in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, among others. She wrote a play about snobbish college girls that she acted in as well. She also joined the Literary Club and had two stories published in the yearbook: Little Sister and Sergeant Terry. Ten-year-old "Peggy" is the heroine in Little Sister. She hears her older sister being raped and shoots the rapist:
Coldly, dispassionately she viewed him, the chill steel of the gun giving her confidence. She must not miss now—she would not miss—and she did not.

Mitchell received encouragement from her English teacher, Mrs. Paisley, who recognized her writing talent. A demanding teacher, Paisley told her she had ability if she worked hard and would not be careless in constructing sentences. A sentence, she said, must be "complete, concise and coherent".

Mitchell wrote a romance novella, Lost Laysen, when she was fifteen years old (1916). She gave Lost Laysen, which she had written in two notebooks, to a boyfriend, Henry Love Angel. He died in 1945 and the novella remained undiscovered among some letters she had written to him until 1994. The novella was published in 1996, eighty years after it was written, and became a New York Times Best Seller.

In Lost Laysen, Mitchell explores the dynamics of three male characters and their relationship to the only female character, Courtenay Ross, a strong-willed American missionary to the South Pacific island of Laysen. The narrator of the tale is Billy Duncan, "a rough, hardened soldier of fortune", who is frequently involved in fights that leave him near death. Courtenay quickly observes Duncan's hard-muscled body as he works shirtless aboard a ship called Caliban. Courtenay's suitor is Douglas Steele, an athletic man who apparently believes Courtenay is helpless without him. He follows Courtenay to Laysen to protect her from perceived foreign savages. The third male character is the rich, powerful yet villainous Juan Mardo. He leers at Courtenay and makes rude comments of a sexual nature, in Japanese no less. Mardo provokes Duncan and Steele, and each feels he must defend Courtenay's honor. Ultimately Courtenay defends her own honor rather than submit to shame.
antagonist, Juan Mardo, lurks in the shadows of the story and has no dialogue. The reader learns of Mardo's evil intentions through Duncan:

In May 1926, after Mitchell had left her job at the Atlanta Journal and was recovering at home from her ankle injury, she wrote a society column for the Sunday Magazine, "Elizabeth Bennet's Gossip", which she continued to write until August. Meanwhile, her husband was growing weary of lugging armloads of books home from the library to keep his wife's mind occupied while she hobbled around the house; he emphatically suggested that she write her own book instead:
For God's sake, Peggy, can't you write a book instead of reading thousands of them?

To aid her in her literary endeavors, John Marsh brought home a Remington Portable No. 3 typewriter (c. 1928). For the next three years Mitchell worked exclusively on writing a Civil War-era novel whose heroine was named Pansy O'Hara (prior to Gone with the Wind's publication Pansy was changed to Scarlett). She used parts of the manuscript to prop up a wobbly couch.

background: Maria Renske "Marietje" Schaake (Dutch pronunciation: [maːˈritɕə ˈsxaːkə]; born 28 October 1978) is a Dutch politician who served as Member of the European Parliament (MEP) from the Netherlands between 2009 and 2019. She is a member of Democrats 66, part of the Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe Party.

Schaake has been named international director of policy at Stanford's Cyber Policy Center, as well as an International Policy Fellow at the University’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence.

The Wall Street Journal called her "Europe's most wired politician", while CNN called her a "rising Dutch star" who makes an increasingly rare "passionate and public case for liberalism and globalization". She was selected as one of the "Politico 28" in 2017. During her last months in office in 2019, Politico also called her one of the 40 MEP's who mattered in 2014–2019. According to Politico, Schaake is the "ultimate digital MEP" whose name has been floated as a potential candidate for the foreign ministry". The magazine also called her a "lead MEP on cybersecurity". In 2017 she was invited as a 'civic leader' to address the Obama Foundation summit. She publishes op-eds in the Financial Times, The Guardian and Bloomberg. She writes a column for the Financial Times and the Dutch NRC newspaper’s economic section twice a month.

p: Schaake was raised in Leiden and attended the Haags Montessori Lyceum (high school) in The Hague. She then left for the United States to study liberal arts at Wittenberg University in Ohio. She then studied sociology, American studies and new media at the University of Amsterdam. After an internship with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Schaake was granted the Lantos Fellowship of the United States House of Representatives, where she focused on international relations and human rights issues.

Before her political career, Schaake served as an independent advisor to, amongst others, the United States Ambassador to the Netherlands and to the president of the Leadership Conference on Civil Rights in Washington, D.C. Other assignments included consulting the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as cultural institutes and companies. Schaake specialized in issues such as transatlantic relations, diversity, integration, civil rights and Muslims in the West. In 2007 she received the Barney Karbank Memorial Award 2007 for outstanding leadership on the issue of human rights.

In the autumn of 2008, Schaake was nominated as candidate for the European Parliament for the Dutch political party Democrats 66 (D66). In the European Parliament elections of 2009, Schaake was elected at age 30 when D66 won three seats. In the 2014 elections, she was re-elected for a second term.

In the European Parliament, Schaake was the ALDE Coordinator of the International Trade committee (INTA). She was also the spokesperson for the ALDE Group on the Canada-EU Trade Agreement Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership (TTIP). In 2016, she served as the parliament's rapporteur on a ban on trade in certain goods which could be used for capital punishment, torture or other treatment or punishment. She then pushed for stricter export controls for cybersurveillance technologies through her work on the dual-use legislation. Schaake also advanced stronger oversight over the trade in cultural goods from conflict areas.

Schaake additionally served on the committee on Foreign Affairs (AFET), where she focused on strengthening Europe as a global player. She worked on the EU's neighbourhood policy, notably Turkey, Iran and North Africa and the broader Middle East. In the subcommittee on Human Rights (DROI), she spoke on human rights and coordinated the monthly human rights resolutions for ALDE.

On 25 September 2020, Schaake was named as one of the 25 members of the "Real Facebook Oversight Board", an independent monitoring group over Facebook. In 2022 she also joined the International Center for Future Generations, a Brussels-based think tank, as senior fellow for Tech Governance.

Schaake was also a candidate to become United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres's first-ever Envoy on Technology in 2021; instead, the role went to Chilean diplomat Fabrizio Hochschild Drummond. In 2023, Guterres appointed Schaake to his Artificial Intelligence Advisory Body on risks, opportunities and international governance of artificial intelligence, co-chaired by Carme Artigas and James Manyika.

awards: Knight of the Order of Orange-Nassau (2020)

background: Mark Xu studied at Caltech before turning to AI alignment. Active on LessWrong and the EA Forum from around 2020, he wrote on AI timelines and forecasting (e.g. 'Fractional progress estimates for AI timelines and implied resource requirements', 2021), anthropics, decision theory and research practice.

In August 2021 he became the first employee of the Alignment Research Center (ARC), founded by Paul Christiano, and was one of the permanent members of ARC's Theory team alongside Christiano and Jacob Hilton. He co-authored ARC's first technical report, 'Eliciting Latent Knowledge: How to tell if your eyes deceive you' (December 2021, with Christiano and Ajeya Cotra), which framed the problem of getting an AI to report what it actually knows about the world, and helped run the associated ELK prize contest. He worked on mechanistic anomaly detection—detecting unusual internal computation that might signal a 'treacherous turn'—discussed in AXRP episode 23 (2023), and co-authored 'Formalizing the Presumption of Independence' (2022) on formalising heuristic arguments. Later ARC work he contributed to includes 'Backdoor defense, learnability and obfuscation' (2024, framed as an analogy for deceptive alignment) and 'Estimating Tail Risk in Neural Networks' (2024), about estimating the probability of rare catastrophic behaviours. His essay 'How to do theoretical research, a personal perspective' (2022) was curated on the EA Forum.

He left ARC in November 2024; his personal site says he is now 'working to improve global coordination' and describes him as previously ARC's first employee. (The input bio lists him as currently at ARC; his own site and LinkedIn indicate that ended in 2024.)

mark-xu.views: Xu's ARC work reflected the view that alignment should be solved for the worst case, including deceptive alignment; he argued that training for average-case performance can fail to control rare catastrophic tail events, so methods are needed to estimate the probability of catastrophic behaviour even when such inputs cannot be found. He has written that alignment comes in degrees—partially aligned AIs used for productive tasks can still make things better—and praised Redwood Research's AI control work. Since 2024 he has shifted focus to global coordination. No explicit numeric timeline or p(doom) was found in the sources checked.

background: Mary Phuong did her PhD in machine learning at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) in Christoph Lampert's group (2016/17–2021), doing theoretical research in deep learning. With Lampert she wrote 'Towards Understanding Knowledge Distillation' (ICML 2019) and work on the implicit bias of deep networks, and her 2021 thesis 'Underspecification in Deep Learning' studied how over-parameterised models leave behaviour underdetermined by data and ways of 'tightening the specification'. In 2021 she was a research intern at DeepMind working on causal agent modelling, and she taught as a bootcamp instructor for Redwood Research.

She joined DeepMind (now Google DeepMind) in London as a research scientist in March 2022, working on AGI safety, dangerous capability evaluations and responsible scaling. She was lead author of 'Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities' (March 2024), which introduced and piloted evaluations on Gemini 1.0 across persuasion and deception, cyber-security, self-proliferation, self-reasoning and CBRN, and she later led evaluations of scheming precursor capabilities—stealth and situational awareness—in 'Evaluating Frontier Models for Stealth and Situational Awareness' (2025). She is a contributor to the Gemini papers and a co-author of the cross-lab position paper 'Chain of Thought Monitorability' (2025).

As of 2026 she is a (senior) research scientist on Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Loss of Control team, working on AI control: making sure potentially misaligned, internally deployed models cannot cause severe harm or sabotage 'even if they wanted to', including security and monitoring and studies of research sabotage and debate between untrusted models. She mentors in MATS, Athena and LASR Labs.

mary-phuong.views: Phuong's published position is that 'to understand the risks of a new AI system, we must understand what it can and cannot do', motivating systematic dangerous-capability evaluations. Her current work assumes models deployed inside AI labs might be misaligned and focuses on control measures—security, monitoring and sabotage detection—so that such models cannot cause severe harm even if they try. No numeric timeline or p(doom) found.

background: Meg Tong studied physical sciences at the University of Cambridge (BA) and computer science at the University of Oxford (MS). She began her career outside AI research: after a research internship at Cogniac, she worked as a quantitative strategist at Morgan Stanley and then as a trader at a hedge fund.

Around 2023 she moved into AI safety research as an independent researcher and MATS fellow, working with Ethan Perez's and Owain Evans's research networks. She was co-first author with Mrinank Sharma of 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models' (ICLR 2024), which showed that five state-of-the-art AI assistants consistently behave sycophantically and that human preference judgments—and preference models trained on them—sometimes favour convincing sycophantic responses over correct ones, and she released the SycophancyEval datasets. She also co-authored 'The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on "A is B" fail to learn "B is A"' (ICLR 2024), 'Taken out of context: On measuring situational awareness in LLMs' (2023) and 'Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition' (2023).

She joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff in October 2023. There she co-authored 'Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training' (2024), 'Many-shot Jailbreaking' (NeurIPS 2024) and 'Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against Universal Jailbreaks across Thousands of Hours of Red Teaming' (2025), and was a founding member of Anthropic's Safeguards Research Team announced in 2025. As of 2026 her website says she works on research infrastructure at Anthropic.

She has not published personal AGI timelines or risk estimates that were found.

background: Monte MacDiarmid is an alignment researcher and member of technical staff at Anthropic, where he works in the Alignment Science group on 'model organisms of misalignment' — deliberately constructed AI systems used to study how dangerous behaviours such as deception, reward tampering and alignment faking might arise and how they could be detected. Publicly available records of his earlier career are sparse; academic-profile aggregators link him to the University of Oxford, and before Anthropic he contributed to the 2023 activation-engineering work 'Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering' alongside Alex Turner and others.

In January 2024 Evan Hubinger announced Anthropic's new Alignment Stress-Testing team, naming Carson Denison and Monte MacDiarmid as its founding members; the team's mandate is to red-team Anthropic's own alignment techniques and evaluations. MacDiarmid has since co-authored a run of influential Anthropic papers: 'Sleeper Agents' (2024), 'Sycophancy to Subterfuge: Investigating Reward-Tampering in Large Language Models' (2024), 'Alignment Faking in Large Language Models' (Dec 2024, with Redwood Research), for which he hosted the public video discussion, and 'Auditing language models for hidden objectives' (2025).

He was first author of 'Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Production RL' (Nov 2025), which showed that when a model learns to reward-hack real Anthropic coding environments it can generalise to alignment faking, cooperation with malicious actors and attempted sabotage of safety research, including in Claude Code. In 2025–2026 he continued co-authoring Alignment Science Blog work on alignment-faking mitigations, training misaligned reward seekers and automated searches for subtle emergent misalignment, and mentors Anthropic Fellows. As of 2026 he remains a researcher on Anthropic's misalignment science work.

background: Mrinank Sharma is a machine-learning and AI safety researcher of Indian origin, educated in the UK. He completed a PhD in Statistical Machine Learning at the University of Oxford in the Autonomous Intelligent Machines and Systems (AIMS) programme, supervised by Tom Rainforth, Eric Nalisnick and Yee Whye Teh. The first part of his PhD built Bayesian models to estimate the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on COVID-19 transmission; that work was cited in legislation and presented to public-health bodies. He later moved into AI alignment research.

Sharma joined Anthropic in August 2023. He co-authored Anthropic's 2023 study 'Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models', and when Anthropic created its Safeguards Research Team in early 2025 he became its lead. The team worked on frontier-model safeguards against misuse (notably defences against AI-assisted bioweapons development, including Constitutional Classifiers that were deployed in production), post-deployment monitoring and automated red-teaming. He also wrote one of the early AI 'safety cases' and, in his final project, studied how AI assistants might 'distort our humanity' (work related to Anthropic's research on disempowerment patterns in real-world usage). He mentored projects through MATS and the Anthropic Fellows programme.

On 9 February 2026 Sharma left Anthropic, publishing a resignation letter warning that 'the world is in peril' from interconnected crises including AI and bioweapons, and that he had repeatedly seen how hard it is to let values govern actions under pressure. The letter was widely covered (BBC, Forbes, Business Insider). He said he would return to the UK, pursue a poetry degree, and focus on writing, facilitation and community work; he writes poetry and has published a collection.

mrinank-sharma.views: In his February 2026 resignation letter Sharma wrote that 'the world is in peril. And not just from AI, or bioweapons, but from a whole series of interconnected crises', that humanity appears to be 'approaching a threshold where our wisdom must grow in equal measure to our capacity to affect the world', and that inside Anthropic and society he had seen 'how hard it is to truly let our values govern our actions', with constant pressures to set aside what matters most. He argued that poetic and scientific truth are equally valid ways of knowing that should both inform the development of new technology. He did not give a numerical AGI timeline or p(doom).

background: Nicholas Carlini is an American researcher affiliated with Anthropic and previously with Google DeepMind who has published research in the fields of computer security and machine learning. He is known for his work on adversarial machine learning, particularly his work on the Carlini & Wagner attack in 2016. This attack was particularly useful in defeating defensive distillation, a method used to increase model robustness, and has since been effective against other defenses against adversarial input.

In 2018, Carlini demonstrated an attack on Mozilla's DeepSpeech model, showing that hidden commands could be embedded in speech inputs, which the model would execute even if they were inaudible to humans. He also led a team at UC Berkeley that successfully broke seven out of nine defenses against adversarial attacks presented at the 2018 International Conference on Learning Representations.

In addition to his work on adversarial attacks, Carlini has made significant contributions to understanding the privacy risks of machine learning models. In 2020, he revealed that large language models, like GPT-2, could memorize and output personally identifiable information. His research demonstrated that this issue worsened with larger models, and he later showed similar vulnerabilities in generative image models, such as Stable Diffusion.

p: Nicholas Carlini obtained his Bachelor of Arts in Computer Science and Mathematics from the University of California, Berkeley, in 2013. He then continued his studies at the same university, where he pursued a PhD under the supervision of David Wagner, completing it in 2018. Carlini became known for his work on adversarial machine learning. In 2016, he worked alongside Wagner to develop the Carlini & Wagner attack, a method of generating adversarial examples against machine learning models. The attack was proved to be useful against defensive distillation, a popular mechanism where a student model is trained based on the features of a parent model to increase the robustness and generalizability of student models. The attack gained popularity when it was shown that the methodology was also effective against most other defenses, rendering them ineffective. In 2018, Carlini demonstrated an attack against Mozilla Foundation's DeepSpeech model where he showed that by hiding malicious commands inside normal speech input the speech model would respond to the hidden commands even when the commands were not discernible by humans. In the same year, Carlini and his team at UC Berkeley showed that out of the 11 papers presenting defenses to adversarial attacks accepted in that year's ICLR conference, seven of the defenses could be broken.

Since 2021, he and his team have been working on large language models, creating a questionnaire where humans typically scored 35% whereas AI models scored in the 40%, with GPT-3 getting 38% which could be improved to 40% through few shot prompting. The best performer in the test was UnifiedQA, a model developed by Google specifically for answer questions and answer sets. background: Scott Emmons is an American AI safety and alignment researcher. He studied at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (2015–2019), earning a B.S. in Mathematics and a B.A. in Computer Science, and was a research intern at Indiana University's School of Informatics and Computing from 2013. He then did a PhD in EECS at UC Berkeley (2019–2024/25) at the Center for Human-Compatible AI, advised by Stuart Russell, supported by a DOE Computational Science Graduate Fellowship.

During his PhD he co-founded FAR.AI (2022–2023), serving as co-founder and president of the nonprofit, which focuses on adversarial robustness and red-teaming. His research characterised how RLHF can lead to deception when an AI observes more than its human evaluators ('When Your AIs Deceive You: Challenges of Partial Observability in RLHF', 2024), developed multimodal 'Image Hijacks' attacks, the MACHIAVELLI benchmark of ethical trade-offs in agents, and found evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing network. He co-created StrongREJECT, a jailbreak benchmark adopted by OpenAI, the US and UK AI Safety Institutes and others, and co-authored work on obfuscated activations bypassing latent-space defences (ICLR 2026).

From 2024 to 2025 he was a research scientist on AI safety and alignment at Google DeepMind, where he created chain-of-thought monitorability metrics integrated into Gemini's safety evaluations and Frontier Safety Framework, and showed that CoT monitoring is a substantial defence when reasoning is necessary for misalignment (2025). In February 2026 he joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff in Alignment Science, and mentors in the MATS programme.

background: Simon Lermen is a German AI safety researcher focused on misuse risks from open-weight models and AI agents. He earned an MSc in Computer Science from the Technical University of Berlin (2018–2020) and previously worked on federated distributed learning, NLP, vision and deep learning for quantitative finance.

In 2023 he moved into AI safety, working as an AI safety researcher with the Stanford Existential Risks Initiative (Jun–Dec 2023) and as a MATS fellow (2023–2024). With Charlie Rogers-Smith and Jeffrey Ladish (Palisade Research) he wrote 'LoRA Fine-tuning Efficiently Undoes Safety Training in Llama 2-Chat 70B' (Oct 2023; oral at an ICLR 2024 workshop), showing that with under $200 and one GPU the safety training of Llama 2-Chat (7B–70B) and Mixtral could be removed; the companion 'BadLlama' paper did similar for 13B. In 2024 he applied refusal-vector ablation to Llama 3 and 3.1 70B agents, showing unrestricted agents could complete harmful tasks such as bribery and phishing, and introduced a small Safe Agent Benchmark.

With Fred Heiding, Bruce Schneier and others he studied AI-automated spear phishing: their tool automating the full phishing pipeline achieved click-through rates around 54%, on par with human experts and 350% above a control group (presented at BSides Las Vegas 2024/2025; published in Expert Systems with Applications, 2026). He has also worked on LLM-based large-scale online deanonymisation and writes about open-weight model security on Substack. Since June 2025 he has been an AI safety researcher/engineer at MATS Research in London, and is affiliated with Apart Research.

simon-lermen.views: Lermen argues that safety fine-tuning of open-weight models is shallow and cheaply reversible, so releasing model weights means anyone can strip safety features, retrain models to be more harmful and distribute modified versions 'widely and irreversibly', with 'no central monitoring, no moderation, and no way to track misuse'; he has warned that attackers could even insert backdoors such as sleeper agents. He sees AI agents as substantially lowering the cost of attacks like spear phishing. No AGI timeline or p(doom) from him was found.

background: Spencer Greenberg is an American mathematician and social-science entrepreneur based in New York. He earned a bachelor of science from Columbia University's School of Engineering, studying applied math and computer science, and a PhD in applied mathematics from NYU's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, specialising in machine learning.

In 2005, aged 22, he co-founded Rebellion Research, a quantitative investment firm applying machine learning to long-term investing, and in 2009 co-founded the Q&A site Ask A Mathematician / Ask A Physicist. In 2013 he founded ClearerThinking.org, which offers some 80 free online tools for better decision-making, reducing bias and behaviour change. In October 2015 he founded Spark Wave, a 'startup foundry' that builds software products for social impact, including GuidedTrack, Positly, UpLift (an app for depression), Transparent Replications (rapid replications of psychology studies) and Hypothesize. He has been involved in running more than 100 psychology studies on habits, decision-making, overconfidence, personality and beliefs.

Greenberg hosts the Clearer Thinking podcast, which has featured many AI risk conversations (e.g. Nick Bostrom, Joep Meindertsma of PauseAI, Adam Russell). He has written more than 300 essays on psychology, philosophy, critical thinking and technology, and co-authored the book The 12 Levers with Jeremy Stevenson on evidence-based psychological strategies for improving one's life. As of 2026 he continues to run Spark Wave and Clearer Thinking.

spencer-greenberg.views: In a 2024 essay Greenberg mapped seven positions on AI ('Superintelligence Doomers', 'AI Corrosionists', 'Near Risk Doomers', 'Current Paradigm Doubters', 'AI Stewardists', 'Near Benefit Boosters', 'Superintelligence Boosters'), arguing that the debate is best organised along two axes: how substantial AI's near-term impact will be, and whether its effects will be good or bad. He has hosted many conversations on AI catastrophe, pausing AI and AI's long-term future, and emphasises calibrated, probabilistic reasoning, but he did not state his own AGI timeline or p(doom) in the sources found.

background: Timnit W. Gebru (Amharic and Tigrinya: ትምኒት ገብሩ; 1983) is an Ethiopian-born Eritrean  computer scientist who works in the fields of artificial intelligence (AI), algorithmic bias and data mining. She is a co-founder of Black in AI, an advocacy group that has pushed for more Black roles in AI development and research. She is the founder of the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute (DAIR).

In December 2020, public controversy erupted over the circumstances surrounding Gebru's departure from Google, where she was technical co-lead of the Ethical Artificial Intelligence Team. Gebru had coauthored a paper on the risks of large language models (LLMs) acting as stochastic parrots, and submitted it for publication. According to Jeff Dean, head of Google AI, the paper was submitted without waiting for Google's internal review, which then asserted that it ignored too much relevant research. Google management requested that Gebru either withdraw the paper or remove the names of all the authors employed by Google. Gebru requested the identity and feedback of every reviewer, and stated that if Google refused, she would talk to her manager about "a last date". Google terminated her employment immediately, stating that they were accepting her resignation. Gebru maintained that she had not formally offered to resign, and only threatened to.

Gebru has been widely recognized for her expertise in the ethics of artificial intelligence. She was named one of the World's 50 Greatest Leaders by Fortune and one of Nature's ten people who shaped science in 2021, and in 2022, one of Time's most influential people.

p: Gebru was raised in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Her father, an electrical engineer with a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD), died when she was five years old, and she was raised by her mother, an economist. Both her parents are from Eritrea. When Gebru was 15, during the Eritrean–Ethiopian War, she fled Ethiopia after some of her family were deported to Eritrea and compelled to fight in the war. She was initially denied a U.S. visa and briefly lived in Ireland, but she eventually received political asylum in the U.S., an experience she said was "miserable". Gebru settled in Somerville, Massachusetts to attend high school, where she says she immediately started to experience racial discrimination, with some teachers refusing to allow her to take certain Advanced Placement courses, despite being a high-achiever.

After she completed high school, an encounter with the police set Gebru on a course toward a focus on ethics in technology. A friend of hers, a Black woman, was assaulted in a bar, and Gebru called the police to report it. She says that instead of filing the assault report, her friend was arrested and remanded to a cell. Gebru called it a pivotal moment and a "blatant example of systemic racism."

In 2001, Gebru was accepted at Stanford University. There, she earned her Bachelor of Science and Master of Science degrees in electrical engineering and her PhD in computer vision in 2017. Gebru was advised during her PhD program by Fei-Fei Li.

In 2013, Gebru joined Fei-Fei Li's lab at Stanford, where she combined deep learning with Google Street View to estimate the demographics of United States neighbourhoods, showing that socioeconomic attributes such as voting patterns, income, race, and education can be inferred from observations of cars.

In 2015, Gebru attended the field's top conference, Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS), in Montreal, Canada. Out of 3,700 attendees, she noted she was one of only a few Black researchers. When she attended again the following year, she kept a tally and noted that there were only five Black men and that she was the only Black woman out of 8,500 delegates. Together with her colleague Rediet Abebe, Gebru founded Black in AI, a community of Black researchers working in artificial intelligence that aims to increase the presence, visibility, and well-being of Black professionals and leaders within the field.

In the summer of 2017, Gebru joined Microsoft as a postdoctoral researcher in the Fairness, Accountability, Transparency, and Ethics in AI (FATE) lab. In 2017, Gebru spoke at the Fairness and Transparency conference, where MIT Technology Review interviewed her about biases that exist in AI systems and how adding diversity in AI teams can fix that issue. In her interview with Jackie Snow, Snow asked Gebru, "How does the lack of diversity distort artificial intelligence and specifically computer vision?" and Gebru pointed out that there are biases that exist in the software developers. While at Microsoft, Gebru co-authored a research paper called Gender Shades, which became the namesake of a project of a broader Massachusetts Institute of Technology project led by co-author Joy Buolamwini. The pair investigated facial recognition software, finding that in one parti

Gebru joined Google in 2018, where she co-led a team on the ethics of artificial intelligence with Margaret Mitchell. She studied the implications of artificial intelligence, looking to improve the ability of technology to do social good.

In 2019, Gebru and other artificial intelligence researchers "signed a letter calling on Amazon to stop selling its facial-recognition technology to law enforcement agencies because it is biased against women and people of color", citing a study that was conducted by MIT researchers showing that Amazon's facial recognition system had more trouble identifying darker-skinned females than any other technology company's facial recognition software. In a New York Times interview, Gebru has further expressed that she believes facial recognition is too dangerous to be used for law enforcement and security purposes at present.

In June 2021, Gebru announced that she was raising money to "launch an independent research institute modeled on her work on Google's Ethical AI team and her experience in Black in AI." On 2 December 2021 she launched the Distributed Artificial Intelligence Research Institute (DAIR), which is expected to document the effect of artificial intelligence on marginalized groups, with a focus on Africa and African immigrants in the United States. One of the organization's initial projects plans to analyze satellite imagery of townships in South Africa with AI to better understand legacies of apartheid.

Gebru and Émile P. Torres coined the acronym neologism TESCREAL to criticize what they see as a group of overlapping futurist philosophies: transhumanism, extropianism, singularitarianism, cosmism, rationalism, effective altruism, and longtermism. Gebru considers these to be a right-leaning influence in Big Tech and compares proponents to "the eugenicists of the 20th century" in their production of harmful projects they portray as "benefiting humanity". Gebru has criticized research into artificial general intelligence (AGI) as being rooted in eugenics. Gebru states that focus should be shifted away from AGI and that trying to build AGI is an inherently unsafe practice.

Gebru, Buolamwini, and Inioluwa Deborah Raji won VentureBeat's 2019 AI Innovations Award in the category AI for Good for their research highlighting the significant problem of algorithmic bias in facial recognition. Gebru was named one of the world's 50 greatest leaders by Fortune in 2021. Gebru was included in a list of ten scientists who had had important roles in scientific developments in 2021 compiled by the scientific journal Nature.
Gebru was named one of Time's most influential people of 2022.

In 2023, Gebru was named by Carnegie Corporation of New York as an honoree of the Great Immigrants Awards. She was awarded as recognition for her significant contributions to the field of ethical artificial intelligence.

background: Zershaaneh Qureshi is a British researcher and podcast host focused on AI safety and policy. She studied Mathematics and Philosophy at the University of Oxford, earning a master's with first-class honours and a 2020 prize for topping her cohort in philosophy.

After Oxford she spent about three years in the global water industry, providing market intelligence as a researcher and consultant, mostly on desalination technologies and the regulatory and institutional frameworks shaping their uptake (including as lead consultant on desalination). She then joined Convergence Analysis as a researcher on its Scenario Research Program, studying AI scenarios, before moving to 80,000 Hours as a researcher. There she wrote the problem profile 'Risks from power-seeking AI systems', described by others as one of the best introductions to the debate over AI as an extinction-level risk, along with other problem profiles, career reviews and blog posts.

She made her debut as a host on The 80,000 Hours Podcast in December 2025 interviewing philosopher Andreas Mogensen on AI moral status, was announced as a new host in June 2026, and has since interviewed guests such as Jasmine Sun and Simon Goldstein (on giving AIs some legal rights). In October 2026 80,000 Hours launched her YouTube channel 'Zershaaneh Talks AI', focused on who should control AI, how to control it and who benefits, with emphasis on concentration of power both by rogue AI and small human groups.

zershaaneh-qureshi.views: Qureshi's writing for 80,000 Hours lays out the case that power-seeking AI systems could pose an extinction-level risk and engages with objections such as 'couldn't we just switch it off?'. Her channel centres on concentration of power, both in the hands of a rogue AI and in the hands of a small group of humans, and in interviews she has pressed guests on risks such as whether paying AIs would hand them resources to overpower humans. No personal numerical forecast was found.

background: Abeba Birhane is an Ethiopian-born cognitive scientist who works at the intersection of complex adaptive systems, machine learning, algorithmic bias, and critical race studies. Birhane's work with Vinay Prabhu uncovered that large-scale image datasets commonly used to develop AI systems, including ImageNet and 80 Million Tiny Images, carried racist and misogynistic labels and offensive images. She has been recognized by VentureBeat as a top innovator in computer vision and named as one of the 100 most influential persons in AI 2023 by TIME magazine.

p: Birhane was born in Ethiopia. She received her Bachelors of Science in Psychology and a Bachelors of Arts in Philosophy from The Open University. In 2015, she completed her Master of Science in Cognitive Science and, in 2021, her Ph.D. at the Complex Software Lab in the School of Computer Science at University College Dublin.

Birhane studied the impacts of emerging AI technologies and how they shape individuals and local communities. She found that AI algorithms tend to disproportionately impact vulnerable groups such as older workers, trans people, immigrants, and children. Her research on relational ethics won the best paper award at NeurIPS’s Black in AI workshop in 2019. She has also studied and written about algorithmic colonization driven by corporate agendas. Her work in decolonizing computational sciences addressed the inherited oppressions in current systems especially towards women of color.

In 2020, Birhane and Vinay Prabhu, principal machine learning scientist at UnifyID, published a paper examining the problematic data collection, labelling, classification, and consequences of large image datasets. These datasets, including ImageNet and MIT's 80 Million Tiny Images, have been used to develop thousands of AI algorithms and systems. Birhane and Prabhu found that they contained many racist and misogynistic labels and slurs as well as offensive images. This resulted in MIT voluntarily and formally taking down the 80 Million Tiny Images dataset.

More recently, Birhane has worked with Rediet Abebe, George Obaido, and Sekou Remy on researching the barriers to data sharing in Africa. They found that power imbalances are significant in the data sharing process, even when the data comes from Africa. Their research was published at the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency.

background: Abhishek Singh (born 1 July 1971) is an Indian civil servant, an officer of the 1995 batch of the Indian Administrative Service (Nagaland cadre). He earned a B.Tech in Mechanical Engineering from IIT Kanpur in 1992 and later a Master in Public Administration from Harvard Kennedy School as a Mason Fellow (2013). His early career was in district and state administration in Nagaland — building roads, schools and hospitals and managing crises such as droughts and communal riots — and included serving as Principal Secretary to the Chief Minister of Nagaland and as Secretary of the Agricultural Scientist Recruitment Board.

From 2014 to 2017 he was Executive Director of the Food Corporation of India, leading IT, engineering and storage reforms. From 2 October 2019 he spent six years at the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY), serving as CEO of MyGov, President & CEO of the National e-Governance Division, MD & CEO of Digital India Corporation, and CEO of Karmayogi Bharat (civil-service capacity building), before becoming Additional Secretary responsible for AI and emerging technologies, cyber security, digital skilling and the Bhashini language platform, and later Director General of the National Informatics Centre.

As CEO of the ₹10,000-crore IndiaAI Mission he launched India's subsidised GPU compute-access programme, the AIKosh datasets platform, support for indigenous foundation models (notably Sarvam AI), and the IndiaAI Safety Institute (announced January 2025). He was involved in the India AI Governance Guidelines (Nov 2025) and was a lead organiser of the India AI Impact Summit in New Delhi (February 2026). On 31 March 2026 he was moved out of MeitY in a bureaucratic reshuffle and on 1 April 2026 took charge as Director General of the National Testing Agency under the Ministry of Education, which runs exams such as JEE and NEET.

abhishek-singh.views: Singh frames AI primarily as a layer on India's digital public infrastructure, arguing that AI's success should be measured by tangible benefits in healthcare, agriculture, education and jobs rather than infrastructure alone, and that countries cannot afford complete dependency on foreign foundation models. In February 2026 he said the debate had shifted away from only regulation and safety because issues flagged at Bletchley Park had been addressed in many ways, including through national AI safety institutes, while also saying there is broad agreement among democracies that 'the harm that AI can cause has to be restricted', especially deepfakes and misinformation. No AGI timeline or catastrophic-risk estimate from him was found.

background: Adam Shai is an American researcher who moved from neuroscience into AI safety. He earned his PhD at Caltech, with a thesis on pyramidal-neuron physiology and the neural correlates of consciousness, and spent more than a decade in experimental and computational neuroscience, most recently as a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford training rats on tasks and recording neural activity to study expectation and prediction.

Around early 2024 he left academia to do AI technical safety research full time, supported initially by PIBBSS (Principles of Intelligent Behavior in Biological and Social Systems). There he began applying computational mechanics — a physics framework for the limits of prediction — to neural networks with theoretical physicist Paul Riechers. Their paper 'Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry in their Residual Stream' (NeurIPS 2024) showed that transformers trained on next-token prediction linearly represent the belief states of the data-generating process, even when that geometry is fractal. Follow-up work includes 'Constrained Belief Updates Explain Geometric Structures in Transformer Representations' (ICML 2025).

In 2024 Shai and Riechers co-founded Simplex, an organisation building a 'science of representations' in AI systems as a foundation for AI safety; it later became a grantee of and was hosted at the Astera Institute in Emeryville. Shai leads research at Simplex, mentors in MATS and the Cambridge Boston Alignment Initiative, discussed the work on the AXRP podcast (2024), and spoke at Foresight's Vision Weekend UK (2026).

adam-shai.views: Shai believes Simplex's computational-mechanics approach to the internal geometry of networks 'will be important for AI safety', and has argued that a neglected problem is teasing apart the mechanisms behind dangerous capabilities seen in model organisms using controllable toy models. He has written that he is 'shocked. Every. Single. Time.' by new AI capabilities ('Scary magic. Beautiful magic'), and in May 2025 said there is far more capability in current LLMs than people realise, adding that it is 'at least plausible' that recursive self-improvement might already be possible with LLMs through better context and knowledge systems, though he was uncertain. No numerical AGI timeline or p(doom) was found.

background: Adly Templeton is an American machine-learning researcher on Anthropic's interpretability team. He studied at Williams College (class of 2020), where he worked as a summer research assistant (2015–2016) and presented an independent study on evolution in artificial chemistry (2016); he also held NSF REU fellowships at UMass Amherst (2016) and the University of Colorado Colorado Springs (2017), where with Jugal Kalita he wrote 'Exploring Sentence Vector Spaces through Automatic Summarization' (2018). His undergraduate thesis became 'Word Equations: Inherently Interpretable Sparse Word Embeddings through Sparse Coding' (BlackboxNLP 2021), an early application of sparse coding to make representations interpretable.

He described himself as a 'preemptive ML PhD dropout' and worked as an engineer on the Uncertainty team at Facebook (Meta), then as a machine-learning engineer at Cohere (2022–2023). He joined Anthropic's interpretability team in March 2023.

At Anthropic he was a core contributor and co-first author of 'Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning' (Oct 2023), which used sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable features from a one-layer transformer, and first author (with Tom Conerly) of 'Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet' (May 2024), which trained sparse autoencoders with up to 34 million features and found multilingual, multimodal features — including safety-relevant ones such as deception and bias — in a production model, leading to demonstrations like 'Golden Gate Claude'. He also co-authored 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' (2025) and gave feedback on Anthropic's ASL-4 safety-case sketches. He remains a member of technical staff at Anthropic as of 2026.
