His published work with Anthropic's interpretability team is motivated by the view that understanding models' internal features (including safety-relevant features such as deception, sycophancy and dangerous content) is a route to making AI systems safer.

background: Akiko Murakami (村上明子) is a Japanese AI researcher and executive. She received a master's degree in applied physics from Waseda University's graduate school in 1999, where she researched metal physical properties, and then joined IBM Japan's Tokyo Research Laboratory. Over about 16 years at IBM Research she worked on natural language processing, especially information extraction, text mining and social-media analysis, becoming an advisory researcher; she also translated several technical books on NLP and information retrieval into Japanese. In January 2016 she moved to IBM's Tokyo Software Development Laboratory, where she represented Watson development in Japan.

In April 2021 she joined Sompo Japan Insurance to lead digital transformation, becoming head of its DX Promotion Department, Executive Officer and Chief Digital Officer (April 2022), and Executive Officer and Chief Data Officer heading data-driven management (April 2024). Since April 2025 she has been Executive Vice President and Group Chief Data Officer of Sompo Holdings.

In February 2024 she was appointed (in a part-time capacity) the first Executive Director of the Japan AI Safety Institute (J-AISI), launched on 14 February 2024 within the Information-technology Promotion Agency (IPA). Under her the institute has worked on AI safety evaluation methods, red-teaming guidance, test-bed frameworks and international collaboration with the US and UK AISIs and the international network of safety institutes. She has also served as deputy chair of the Cabinet Office's AI policy study group, a board member of the Association for Natural Language Processing, a Keidanren digital-economy committee member, and a founding member and auditor of the disaster-response IT volunteer group IT DART.

akiko-murakami.views: Murakami argues that ensuring AI safety is essential for promoting the widespread adoption and use of AI, and that the Japan AISI's role is not only to create guidelines but to build red-teaming and test-bed frameworks, develop practical benchmarks with the private sector and collaborate internationally. In a November 2025 Weekly Economist interview on AGI and 'runaway AI' she stressed that it is important to keep up countermeasures against AI running out of control. She frames safety and trust as a blueprint that accelerates innovation. No numerical AGI timeline was found.

background: Alondra Nelson (born April 22, 1968) is an American academic, policy advisor, non-profit administrator, and writer. She is the Harold F. Linder chair and professor in the School of Social Science at the Institute for Advanced Study, an independent research center in Princeton, New Jersey. Since March 2023, she has been a distinguished senior fellow at the Center for American Progress. In October 2023, she was nominated by the Biden-Harris Administration and appointed by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres to the UN High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence.

From 2021 to 2023, Nelson was deputy assistant to President Joe Biden and principal deputy director for science and society of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP), where she performed the duties of the director from February to October 2022. She was the first African American and first woman of color to lead OSTP. Prior to her role in the Biden Administration, she served for four years as president and CEO of the Social Science Research Council, an independent, nonpartisan international nonprofit organization. Nelson was previously professor of sociology at Columbia University, where she served as the inaugural Dean of Social Science, as well as director of the Institute for Research on Women and Gender. She began her academic career on the faculty of Yale University.

She has authored or edited articles, essays, and books including The Social Life of DNA: Race, Reparations, and Reconciliation after the Genome (2016). She is on the advisory board of the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society.

p: In 1994, Nelson earned a Bachelor of Science degree in anthropology, magna cum laude, from the University of California, San Diego. While there, she was elected to Phi Beta Kappa. She earned a Ph.D. in American studies from New York University in 2003. Nelson has received honorary degrees from Amherst College, Northeastern University, Rutgers University, and the City College of New York.
From fall 1999 to spring 2001, Nelson was the New York University Minority Dissertation Fellow in the Department of American Studies at Skidmore College.

From 2003 to 2009, Nelson was an assistant professor and associate professor of African American studies and sociology at Yale University, where she was the recipient of the Poorvu Award for Interdisciplinary Teaching Excellence and a Faculty Fellow in Trumbull College. At Yale, Nelson was the first African American woman to join the Department of Sociology faculty since the department's founding 128 years earlier.

Nelson was recruited to Columbia from Yale in 2009 as an associate professor of sociology and gender studies. She was the first African American to be tenured in the Department of Sociology at this institution. At Columbia, she directed the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (now the Institute for Gender and Sexuality), founded the Columbia University Women's, Gender, and Sexuality Council, and served as the first Dean of Social Science for the Faculty of Arts and Sciences. As dean, Nelson led the first strategic planning process for the social sciences at Columbia University, successfully restructured the Institute for Social and Economic Research and Policy, and helped to establish several initiatives, including the Atlantic Fellows for Racial Equity program, the Eric J. Holder Initiative for Civil and Political Rights, the June Jordan Fellowship Program, the Precision Medicine and Society Program, and the Sabancı Center for Turkish Studies. She left the Columbia University faculty in June 2019 to assume the Harold F. Linder chair and professorship at the Institute for Advanced Study, "the Princeton, New Jersey, organization that once housed the likes of Albert Einstein and J. Robert Oppenheimer."

She has played a prominent role in shaping artificial intelligence (AI) governance, ethics, and public policy at national and international levels. In 2023, she was named to TIME’s inaugural TIME100 AI list, which recognizes the 100 most influential individuals shaping the future of artificial intelligence, citing her leadership in public-interest–oriented AI policy. During her tenure at OSTP, Nelson led the development of the Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, a framework designed to guide governments and technology developers in protecting civil rights, civil liberties, and democratic values in the deployment of automated systems.

In 2023, Nelson introduced the concept of “thick alignment” in discussions of artificial intelligence safety and ethics, drawing on philosophical and anthropological ideas of “thick description." The concept emphasizes sociotechnical analyses that account for contextual, cultural, and value-laden dimensions of human life, rather than narrowly defined technical objectives. A thick alignment perspective argues that AI systems should be designed and governed in ways that reflect complex human values, intentions, and diverse social contexts.

Nelson was nominated by the White House and appointed by United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres as the United States representative to the United Nations High-Level Advisory Body on Artificial Intelligence, a multidisciplinary group tasked with advancing international cooperation and inclusive global governance of AI. She was a key participant in the AI Safety Summit held at Bletchley Park in the United Kingdom in 2023, the first global summit convened to address the risks and governance challenges associated with advanced AI systems. Nelson later served on the Steering Committee of the AI Action

Nelson writes and lectures widely on the intersection of science, technology, medicine, and social inequality. She has published articles, essay, and books, including, most recently, ''The Social Life of DNA: Race, Reparations, and Reconciliation after the Genome.'' Nelson has also written extensively about genetics, genomics, race, and racialization. "At its core, her philosophy was that focusing solely on those communities' exclusion not just misread the past, but shriveled the future possibilities innovation holds for them," Politico noted.

Nelson's writing and commentary have appeared in The New York Times, The Washington Post, Foreign Affairs, The Boston Globe, The Guardian (London),  and The Chronicle of Higher Education, among other publications.
Nelson has received several awards, honors, and distinctions:
Phi Beta Kappa, University of California, San Diego, 1994
Henry Mitchell MacCracken Fellowship and Dean's Fellowship, New York University, 1995

background: Amit Sheth is an Indian computer scientist who works at University of South Carolina in Columbia, South Carolina. He holds the NCR Chair and is a Professor of Computer Science and Engineering, and is the founding Director of the Artificial Intelligence Institute of South Carolina (AIISC). From 2007 to June 2019, he was the LexisNexis Ohio Eminent Scholar, director of the Ohio Center of Excellence in Knowledge-enabled Computing, and a professor of Computer Science at Wright State University. Sheth's work has been cited by over 64,800 publications. He has an h-index of 122. Research.com ranked him among the top 50 computer science researchers in the United States and top 80 worldwide in its 2022 edition.

p: Sheth received his bachelor's in engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in computer science in 1981. He received his M.S. and Ph.D. in computer science from Ohio State University in 1983 and 1985, respectively.

Since joining the University of South Carolina, Sheth has pursued a research agenda centered on knowledge-empowered neurosymbolic and hybrid AI. He introduced the concept of "Computing for Human Experience," describing how semantics-empowered technologies can enrich and support human activities across physical, cyber, and social domains. His research addresses grounding, alignment, instructability, analogical reasoning, interpretability, explainability, and trustworthy AI, as well as multimodal and conversational AI. Among the research concepts he introduced is Knowledge-infused Learning, a framework for integrating external knowledge into machine learning to improve interpretability and safety. He has also introduced the terms Smart Data, Citizen Sensing, Semantic Perception, and Augmented Personalized Health. AIISC has conducted interdisciplinary research spanning digital and connected health, mental health and wellbeing, biomedical informatics, smart manufacturing, education, and the mitigation of online disinformation and radicalization, with research partnerships across eight colleges and schools at the university.

background: Arthur Conmy is a British AI researcher (born c. 2001) based in London. He studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating with upper first-class honours, and did a software engineering internship at Meta in 2021.

In 2022–2023 he worked at Redwood Research, where he contributed to foundational mechanistic-interpretability work: 'Interpretability in the Wild', which identified the indirect-object-identification (IOI) circuit in GPT-2 Small, and, as first author, 'Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability' (ACDC, NeurIPS 2023 spotlight), which automates finding the subgraph of a model responsible for a behaviour. He also co-authored work on copy suppression and successor heads.

From October 2023 to June 2026 he was a (senior) research engineer at Google DeepMind on the AI Safety & Alignment team and Neel Nanda's language-model interpretability team. He was one of two key engineers who shipped activation probes into Gemini 2.5 deployments (live on AI Overviews from April 2025, including cyber-misuse probes), worked on Gemini post-training, reward-model bias discovery and reasoning behaviour, and co-developed Gated SAEs and the open Gemma Scope sparse-autoencoder suites (1 and 2), as well as SAEBench. He has mentored in MATS since MATS 6.0, producing papers on chain-of-thought faithfulness, 'Thought Anchors' and subliminal learning. In June 2026 he announced he was joining Anthropic (and moving to San Francisco) as a member of technical staff to work on aligning upcoming models as they are trained.

arthur-conmy.views: Conmy says his main motivation is 'making the future of AI go well'. Announcing his move to Anthropic in June 2026, he wrote that Claude's capabilities are extraordinary 'but like all models thus far, Claude isn't aligned enough to safely delegate AGI development to', and that aligning models during training should mean triaging signs of misalignment and seeking root-cause fixes rather than 'whack-a-mole patches' such as training against the bad behaviour. He has advocated a pragmatic, practically useful approach to interpretability and a balanced view of when mechanistic interpretability is the right tool. No numerical timeline or p(doom) found.

background: Balaraman Ravindran is an Indian computer scientist and one of India's leading reinforcement-learning researchers. He earned a B.E. from Madurai Kamaraj University and an M.Sc.(Engg.) from the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore; in 1994 he published 'A Survey of Reinforcement Learning', which caught the attention of Andrew Barto, who invited him to UMass Amherst. He did his PhD there (1996–2004) under Barto, with a thesis 'An Algebraic Approach to Abstraction in Reinforcement Learning' introducing MDP homomorphisms.

He joined IIT Madras's Department of Computer Science and Engineering as assistant professor in 2004, becoming associate professor (2009) and full professor (2018). He was founding head of the Robert Bosch Centre for Data Science and AI (2017–), the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI, 2023–) and the Wadhwani School of Data Science and AI, and has headed the Department of Data Science and AI since 2023–2024. He is Mindtree Faculty Fellow, co-director of the RISE group, and has held visiting positions at IISc, the University of Technology Sydney and Google Research Bengaluru (2020–2021). His research spans reinforcement learning (hierarchical and structured RL, safe RL), geometric deep learning, social network analysis and responsible AI. He teaches widely viewed NPTEL RL courses.

He is a Fellow of AAAI and the Indian National Academy of Engineering and an ACM Distinguished Member (2021). In policy, he chaired the committee that drafted the India AI Governance Guidelines (2025), served on the Reserve Bank of India's FREE-AI framework committee, and is an author/expert-advisory contributor to the International AI Safety Report (2025 and 2026 editions) chaired by Yoshua Bengio.

balaraman-ravindran.views: Ravindran emphasises building AI that is 'not only powerful, but also responsible' — transparent, fair and aligned with societal values — and works on algorithms that keep RL agents safe while they learn, which he likens to 'training wheels' for AI. The India AI Governance Guidelines committee he chaired favoured a framework for safe and trustworthy AI that supports innovation rather than heavy new regulation. No personal AGI timeline or p(doom) was found.

background: Been Kim is a South Korean-born computer scientist and one of the founders of modern machine-learning interpretability. She studied at Seoul National University before moving to MIT, where she earned her master's and PhD (2015) working with Julie Shah (and collaborating with Cynthia Rudin and Finale Doshi-Velez) on interactive and interpretable models for human–machine collaboration; her thesis was 'Interactive and Interpretable Machine Learning Models for Human Machine Collaboration', and early work included the Bayesian Case Model (NeurIPS 2014) and a widely covered study of persuasion in meetings.

She then joined Google Brain as a research scientist, rising to senior staff research scientist, and is now a Director and Principal Scientist at Google DeepMind. Her influential contributions include 'Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning' (with Doshi-Velez, 2017), TCAV — Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (ICML 2018), which explains models in terms of human concepts and was showcased by Sundar Pichai at Google I/O 2019 and won a UNESCO Netexplo award — 'Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps' (NeurIPS 2018), Concept Bottleneck Models (ICML 2020), 'Acquisition of Chess Knowledge in AlphaZero' (PNAS 2022) and 'Impossibility Theorems for Feature Attribution' (PNAS 2023). She co-authored DeepMind's 'Model evaluation for extreme risks' (2023).

Her recent work aims to extract new knowledge from superhuman AI and teach it to people: 'Bridging the human–AI knowledge gap through concept discovery and transfer in AlphaZero' (PNAS 2025) taught novel AlphaZero chess concepts to four grandmasters, one of whom became the youngest world chess champion, and she has proposed 'agentic interpretability' and 'neologisms' as new human–AI vocabulary (2025). She gave keynotes at ICLR 2022, ECML 2020 and a G20 meeting, was General Chair of ICLR 2024, sits on the ICLR board, and her work features in Brian Christian's 'The Alignment Problem'.

been-kim.views: Kim says she is 'working to ensure that as machines get smarter, humans do too', and that her work aims to help 'humans to maintain agency by extracting and teaching useful knowledge from AI to humans'. She argues interpretability should treat AI systems as scientific objects to be studied (through observational studies, controlled experiments and 'surgery' on internals) and that the ultimate goal is a shared language enabling humans to learn from and be inspired by AI; she has also shown that popular explanation methods can be unreliable and should be tested. No AGI timeline or p(doom) from her was found.

background: Benjamin Buchanan (born August 21, 2001) is an American professional wrestler. He is signed to WWE where he performs on the Evolve brand under the ring name Brooks Jensen. He is a former one-time and the final NXT UK Tag Team Champion.
Buchanan is a second generation wrestler and is the son of Bull Buchanan, who wrestled with the WWE from 1997 until 2003.

p: Buchanan was born in 2001 in Ranburne, Alabama and is the son of former WWE wrestler Barry Buchanan, who wrestled in the WWE from 1997 to 2003 under the ring names Bull Buchanan and B2.

Buchanan debuted on March 2, 2019. He went on to work throughout the southern wrestling territories, mostly appearing in promotions in Alabama and Georgia. He became a one-time Heavyweight Champion and a multiple-time Tag Team Champion between 2020 and 2021.

background: Ben Shneiderman (born August 21, 1947) is an American computer scientist, a Distinguished University Professor in the University of Maryland Department of Computer Science, which is part of the University of Maryland College of Computer, Mathematical, and Natural Sciences at the University of Maryland, College Park, and the founding director (1983-2000) of the University of Maryland Human-Computer Interaction Lab. He conducted fundamental research in the field of human–computer interaction, developing new ideas, methods, and tools such as the direct manipulation interface, and his eight rules of design.

p: Born in New York, Shneiderman attended the Bronx High School of Science, and received a BS in Mathematics and Physics from the City College of New York in 1968. He then studied at the State University of New York at Stony Brook, where he earned an MS in Computer Science in 1972 and a PhD in 1973.

Shneiderman started his academic career at the State University of New York at Farmingdale in 1968 as an instructor at the Department of Data Processing. In the year before his graduation, he was an instructor in the Department of Computer Science at Stony Brook University (then called the State University of New York at Stony Brook). In 1973, he was appointed assistant professor at the Indiana University Department of Computer Science. In 1976, he moved to the University of Maryland. He started as an assistant professor in the Department of Information Systems Management and became an associate professor in 1979. In 1983, he moved to the Department of Computer Science as an associate professor and was promoted to full professor in 1989. In 1983 he was the Founding Director of its Human-Computer Interaction Lab, which he directed until 2000.

In 2002, his book Leonardo's Laptop: Human Needs and the New Computing Technologies won the IEEE-USA Award for Distinguished Contributions Furthering Public Understanding of the Profession. His 2016 book, The New ABCs of Research: Achieving Breakthrough Collaborations, encourages combining applied and basic research. In 2019, he published Encounters with HCI Pioneers: A Personal History and Photo Journal; in 2022, he published Human-Centered AI.

Shneiderman was inducted as a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery in 1997, a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 2001, a Member of the National Academy of Engineering in 2010, an IEEE Fellow in 2012, and a Fellow of the National Academy of Inventors in 2015. He is an ACM CHI Academy Member and received their Lifetime Achievement Award in 2001. He received the IEEE Visualization Career Award in 2012 and was inducted into the IEEE VIS Academy in 2019. In 2021, he received the InfoVis Conference Test of Time Award with coauthors Ben Bederson and Martin M. Wattenberg.

He received Honorary Doctorates from the University of Guelph (Canada) in 1995, the University of Castile-La Mancha (Spain) in 2010, Stony Brook University in 2015, the University of Melbourne in 2017, Swansea University (in Wales, UK) in 2018, and the University of Pretoria (in South Africa) in 2018.
Shneiderman resides in Bethesda, Maryland. He is the nephew of photographer David Seymour.

In the 1970s, Shneiderman continued to study programmers and the use of flow charts. In the 1977 article "Experimental investigations of the utility of detailed flowcharts in programming", Shneiderman et al. summarized the origin and status quo of flowcharts in computer programming:

Flowcharts have been a part of computer programming since the introduction of computers in the 1940s. In 1947 Goldstein and von Neumann [7] presented a system of describing processes using operation, assertion, and alternative boxes. They felt that "coding begins with the drawing of flow diagram." Prior to coding, the algorithm had been identified and understood. The flowchart represented a high level definition of the solution to be implemented on a machine. Although they were working only with numerical algorithms, they proposed a programming methodology which has since become standard practice in the computer programming field.

Furthermore, Shneiderman had conducted experiments which suggested that flowcharts were not helpful for writing, understanding, or modifying computer programs. At the end of their 1977 paper, Shneiderman et al. concluded:

Later in his career, Shneiderman focused on Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. Shneiderman proposed an alternative vision of AI that emphasized the need for reliable, safe, and trustworthy systems that enable people to benefit from AI's power while remaining in control. Shneiderman emphasized the need for technologies that "augment, amplify, empower, and enhance humans rather than replace them".

background: Benjamin (Ben) Mann is an American software engineer and a co-founder of Anthropic. He earned a B.S. in Computer Science from Columbia University (2007–2011), graduating magna cum laude, and worked as a research associate in Columbia's robotics group. He says reading science fiction and, around 2016, Nick Bostrom's 'Superintelligence' made AI risk real to him. His early career included work at Google (including its Area 120 incubator), a stint of a couple of months at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), and founding a startup (2018–2019).

He joined OpenAI as a member of technical staff in July 2019. On GPT-3 he handled data engineering, model efficiency, the evaluation suite and overlap analysis, was one of the co-first authors of 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners' (2020, listed second after Tom Brown), did demos that helped raise Microsoft's $1 billion investment, built the initial prototype of the OpenAI API and transferred GPT-3 to Azure. He left in December 2020, saying 'safety wasn't the top priority there', and was one of the eight co-founders of Anthropic in early 2021.

At Anthropic he has held some 15 roles — running security for a time, managing operations, starting the product team, and serving as tech lead for product engineering. He founded the Labs (later 'Frontiers') team that transfers research into products, which produced Claude Code and the Model Context Protocol, and as of 2026 co-leads Anthropic Labs.

benjamin-mann.views: Mann said in July 2025 that his '50th percentile chance of hitting some kind of superintelligence is now like 2028', deferring to the Metaculus forecast, and prefers the term 'transformative AI' measured by an 'economic Turing test' (AI passing for ~50% of money-weighted jobs) or world GDP growth above 10% a year. He put the chance of 'an X-risk or extremely bad outcome' from AI at 'somewhere between 0 and 10%', saying things are 'overwhelmingly likely to go well' but that the downside is enormous, that 'once we get to superintelligence, it will be too late to align the models', and that we likely live in a middle world where alignment research is pivotal. He expects major job displacement (engaging with Dario Amodei's 20% unemployment warning) and believes fewer than a thousand people work on safety worldwide.

background: Benjamin (Benji) Rosman is a South African computer scientist who grew up in Johannesburg. He earned B.Sc. (Hons) degrees in Computer Science and in Applied Mathematics at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits), then an M.Sc. in Artificial Intelligence and a PhD in Informatics (2014) at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Perception, Action and Behaviour, supervised by Subramanian Ramamoorthy, with a thesis on learning domain abstractions for long-lived robots.

After his PhD he returned to South Africa, working with the CSIR (receiving its Young Researchers Establishment Fund in 2014) and joining Wits' School of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics, where he rose from lecturer to associate professor and full professor. He runs the Robotics, Autonomous Intelligence and Learning (RAIL) Laboratory, described as Africa's largest AI research lab, directs the National E-Science Postgraduate Teaching and Training Platform, and in November 2024 became founding Director of the Wits Machine Intelligence and Neural Discovery (MIND) Institute, which studies intelligence in machines, humans and animals. His research centres on reinforcement learning and decision making — especially transfer learning, abstraction and composing reusable skills.

Rosman co-founded the Deep Learning Indaba (first held in 2017 with 330 attendees, with communities active in 47 African countries by 2025) and Lelapa AI, a company building AI for African languages, where he has served as Chief Science Officer. He was a 2022–2024 CIFAR Azrieli Global Scholar, became a CIFAR Fellow in Learning in Machines & Brains in 2025, received a Google Faculty Research Award (2018), and was named to the TIME100 Most Influential People in AI list in 2025.

background: Bernhard Schölkopf (born 20 February 1968) is a German computer scientist known for his work in machine learning, especially on kernel methods and causality. He is a director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Tübingen, Germany, where he heads the Department of Empirical Inference. He is also an affiliated professor at ETH Zürich, honorary professor at the University of Tübingen and Technische Universität Berlin, and chairman of the European Laboratory for Learning and Intelligent Systems (ELLIS).

p: Schölkopf studied mathematics, physics, and philosophy in Tübingen and London. He was supported by the Studienstiftung and won the Lionel Cooper Memorial Prize for the best M.Sc. in Mathematics at the University of London. He completed a Diplom in Physics, and then moved to Bell Labs in New Jersey, where he worked with Vladimir Vapnik, who became co-adviser of his PhD thesis at TU Berlin (with Stefan Jähnichen). His thesis, defended in 1997, won the annual award of the German Informatics Association. In 2001, following positions in Berlin, Cambridge and New York, he founded the Department for Empirical Inference at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Cybernetics, which grew into a leading center for research in machine learning. In 2011, he became founding director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems.

With Alex Smola, Schölkopf co-founded the series of Machine Learning Summer Schools. He also co-founded a Cambridge-Tübingen PhD Programme and the Max Planck-ETH Center for Learning Systems. In 2016, he co-founded the Cyber Valley research consortium. He participated in the IEEE Global Initiative on "Ethically Aligned Design".

Schölkopf is co-editor-in-Chief of the Journal of Machine Learning Research, a journal he helped found, being part of a mass resignation of the editorial board of Machine Learning (journal). He is among the world’s most cited computer scientists. Alumni of his lab include Ulrike von Luxburg, Carl Rasmussen, Matthias Hein, Arthur Gretton, Gunnar Rätsch, Matthias Bethge, Stefanie Jegelka, Jason Weston, Olivier Bousquet, Olivier Chapelle, Joaquin Quinonero-Candela, and Sebastian Nowozin.

Schölkopf’s awards include the Royal Society Milner Award and, shared with Isabelle Guyon and Vladimir Vapnik, the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award in the Information and Communication Technologies category. He was the first scientist working in Europe to receive this award. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2026.

background: Carroll Livingston Wainwright (December 2, 1899 – July 6, 1967) was an American artist and socialite.

p: Wainwright was born on December 2, 1899, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, to Stuyvesant Wainwright (1863–1930) and Caroline Smith Snowden (1865–1960). His siblings included Stuyvesant Wainwright (1891–1975) J. Howard Wainwright, and Loudon Snowden Wainwright (1898–1942). After his parents' divorce, his mother remarried to Dr. Carl F. Wolff (1864–1934), and his father remarried to Sarah Hughes.

Wainwright was a nephew of General Jonathan Mayhew Wainwright (1883–1953), a four star-general who was the hero of Bataan and commander of the U.S. forces in the Philippines during World War II. Through his brother, Loudon, he was the uncle of Loudon Wainwright Jr., and the grand-uncle of Loudon Wainwright III, the singer and songwriter, himself the father of Rufus Wainwright, Martha Wainwright, and Lucy Wainwright Roche.

Wainwright's paternal grandparents were Margaret (née Livingston) Wainwright and John Howard Wainwright, who was the son of the Bishop of New York, Jonathan Mayhew Wainwright. His maternal grandparents were Elizabeth Robinson Smith and Archibald Loudon Snowden, who served as U.S. Ambassador to Spain, Serbia, Romania and Greece. He was a direct descendant of Peter Stuyvesant, the last Dutch governor of New York.

After his marriage in 1920, Wainwright became a Wall Street broker. In 1923, he left Wall Street and became a painter, continuing nearly the rest of his life. He focused his art on painting miniatures. In 1927, the family moved to East Hampton, New York, where they built an imposing house called "Gulf Crest," that was valued at $350,000 in 1937.

On May 27, 1920, Wainwright eloped and married 18-year-old Edith Catherine Gould (1900–1937). She was the daughter of millionaire George Jay Gould I (1864-1923) and Edith M. Kingdon (1864-1921). Before their divorce in 1932, they became the parents of:
Stuyvesant Wainwright II (1921–2010), who represented New York's 1st District in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1953 to 1961.
Caroline DePeyster Wainwright (1924–1969), who married Edward T. Shean, an investment banker, in 1945. They divorced in 1963.

background: Dean W. Ball is an American artificial intelligence policy researcher. He graduated from Hamilton College with a BA in history.

In April 2025, Ball joined the Trump administration as the Senior Policy Advisor for Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy. He was the primary author of the administration's AI Action Plan. He left in August 2025 to join the Foundation for American Innovation as a senior fellow. In March 2026, he joined the Heritage Foundation as a visiting fellow.
In July 2026, Ball joined OpenAI as head of strategic futures.

background: Dewi Erwan is a Welsh field-builder in AI safety and biosecurity. Growing up in Wales, he spent seven years as a child actor on the Welsh-language soap opera 'Rownd a Rownd' and came third on Britain's Got Talent with an a cappella group. He studied at Durham University, earning an MEng (BEng Hons) in Mechanical and Electrical / New and Renewable Energy Engineering (2019) and an MA in Risk (International Relations & Geography) in 2020; he was also a director at St Chad's College.

As a student worried about factory farming and climate change, he learned about AI and bioweapon risks. In 2021 he moved to Cambridge, became Executive Director of Effective Altruism Cambridge and Biosecurity Advisor to the Cambridge Existential Risk Initiative (and a founding member of ERA Cambridge), and with Will Saunter turned Cambridge reading groups into the AGI Safety Fundamentals and Biosecurity Fundamentals courses.

In 2022 they founded BlueDot Impact, with Erwan as co-founder and CEO. BlueDot's first AI safety course had about 400 participants; it expanded to AI governance and biosecurity, moved to London, and by 2026 had trained over 10,000 people, with about 1,200 alumni in impactful roles at organisations such as Anthropic, Google DeepMind and the UK AI Security Institute. BlueDot raised $5M in 2024, $25M in 2025 and a total of $71M by 2026 (including $34M from Coefficient Giving), took over Coefficient Giving's career-transition grants programme, and moved its headquarters to San Francisco in 2026, where it is building an in-person campus.

dewi-erwan.views: Erwan argues that 'talent is the bottleneck for AI safety': only around 2,000–3,000 people work full-time on making AI go well while philanthropies with tens of billions cannot deploy capital fast enough. In 2026 he wrote that the world is 'barrelling towards' extreme concentrations of power in AI companies and the US and Chinese governments, democratised bioweapons capability, 'rogue AI swarms' pursuing 'alien desires' and mass job loss, and that there is 'no plan for making AI go well'. BlueDot's stated core belief is that 'AGI could arrive soon, and society is dangerously unprepared', but he remains convinced success is possible if capable people take ownership of key problems. No numerical forecast found.

background: Emmett Shear (born 1983) is an American Internet entrepreneur and investor. He co-founded the live video platform Justin.tv. Shear became the chief executive officer of Twitch when it was spun off from Justin.tv, a position he held until March 2023. In 2011, he was appointed as a part-time partner at venture capital firm Y Combinator. In November 2023, he was briefly the interim CEO of OpenAI.
He is the CEO of AI alignment startup Softmax.

p: Emmett Shear grew up in Seattle, Washington, where he attended the Evergreen School for Gifted Children as well as the Transition School at the University of Washington. There, he met his eventual co-founder Justin Kan at age eight, and the two were bonded by their accelerated math classes and playing Magic: The Gathering.
Shear studied computer science as an undergraduate student at Yale University, and graduated in 2005. He attended with his eventual Twitch co-founders Justin Kan and Michael Seibel.

On November 19, 2023, Shear was named as the interim CEO of OpenAI, following the removal of Sam Altman by the board two days earlier. On November 21, an agreement was reached to reinstate Altman as CEO. It was previously reported that Shear had threatened to resign as CEO if the board could not provide evidence to support Altman's removal.

Shear has publicly stated that he is concerned about the impact AI can have on civilization, estimating his "P(Doom)" (subjective probability of an existential catastrophe from AI such as human extinction) as between 5 and 50 percent.

background: Esben Kran (Esben Kran Christensen) is a Danish AI safety researcher and entrepreneur. He studied cognitive science at Aarhus University (bachelor's, 2019–2022) with time at UC Santa Cruz, worked with Aarhus's Interacting Minds Centre on fNIRS neuroimaging, led NeuroTechX Denmark, and was lead data scientist at the startup EachThing, building NLP models; he has also developed games.

In 2022, aged 22, he left graduate school to found Apart Research, a nonprofit AI safety lab that runs open 'research sprints' (hackathons) and fellowships enabling people anywhere to contribute to AI safety research. As co-director (2023–2025) he grew Apart's community to thousands of participants across 50+ locations and over 20 peer-reviewed papers, including work on neuron interpretation (Neuron to Graph, 2023), language model evaluation, multi-agent security, and DarkBench, a benchmark for manipulative 'dark patterns' in LLMs (oral at ICLR 2025). He also co-authored the Cooperative AI Foundation report 'Multi-agent Risks from Advanced AI' (2025), and is a research affiliate of Denmark's Pioneer Centre for AI.

He has promoted for-profit AI safety, running startup hackathons with Juniper Ventures and Entrepreneur First and co-founding AI Safety Founders (2024). Since November 2024 he has been a partner/advisor at Juniper Ventures, and in 2025 he co-founded Seldon (Seldon Lab), an AGI-security venture lab and fund whose first investments included Andon Labs, Lucid Computing, Workshop Labs and Asymmetric Security. In 2025 he moved from co-director to chairman/board member of Apart Research, and he is based in San Francisco.

esben-kran.views: Kran describes his goal as 'a future with a benevolent relationship between humans and artificial intelligence'. In 2025 short-form writing he argued that 'being obsessed with safety is the only way to win the AI race', that 'hoping AGI will solve all of our problems is irresponsible', and discussed 'the options we have in a fast takeoff world'; he has said he would prefer AGI to be developed under European institutions, which he sees as dedicated to universal human rights. He advocates scaling AI safety through mission-aligned for-profit startups that do not compete with AGI labs, noting AI investment dwarfs safety funding (~$67B vs ~$250M a year). No numerical forecast found.

background: Fernanda Bertini Viégas (born 1971) is a Brazilian computer scientist and graphical designer, whose work focuses on the social, collaborative and artistic aspects of information visualization.

p: Viégas studied graphic design and art history at the University of Kansas, where she obtained her bachelor's degree in 1997. She then moved to the MIT Media Lab, where she received an M.S. in 2000 and a Ph.D. in Media Arts and Sciences in 2005 under the supervision of Judith Donath. The same year she began work at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts, as part of the Visual Communication Lab.

In April 2010, she and Martin M. Wattenberg started a new venture called Flowing Media, Inc., to focus on visualization aimed at consumers and mass audiences. Four months later, both of them joined Google as the co-leaders of the Google's "Big Picture" data visualization group in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

background: Florian Tramèr is a Swiss computer scientist working at the intersection of computer security, privacy, cryptography and machine learning. He earned his M.Sc. in Computer Science at EPFL (2013–2015), where his master's thesis produced FairTest, a toolkit for discovering unfair behaviour in data-driven algorithms, and worked as a scientific assistant with Jean-Pierre Hubaux (2015–2016). As part of this period he co-authored 'Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs' (USENIX Security 2016) with Fan Zhang, Ari Juels and others, which received the USENIX Security Test of Time Award in 2026.

He completed his PhD in Computer Science at Stanford (2016–2021) under Dan Boneh, with a thesis 'Measuring and Enhancing the Security of Machine Learning'. During this time he introduced Ensemble Adversarial Training (ICLR 2018), showed that many proposed adversarial-example defences fail under adaptive attacks, developed systems for private outsourcing of ML using trusted hardware, and co-authored 'Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models' (2021) with Nicholas Carlini and others. He then spent a year as visiting faculty/researcher at Google Brain in Zürich (2021–2022).

In August 2022 he joined ETH Zürich as a tenure-track assistant professor, where he leads the Secure and Private AI (SPY) Lab, studying the worst-case behaviour of large language models and AI agents from an adversarial perspective — including training-data memorisation, poisoning web-scale datasets, stealing parts of production language models, jailbreaks and prompt injection (e.g., the AgentDojo benchmark). In 2024 he co-founded Invariant Labs, an AI-agent security company, and in 2026 he also became a research scientist at Google DeepMind in Zürich. He has received best-paper awards at ICML, NeurIPS and USENIX Security and the AdvML Rising Star Award.

florian-tramer.views: Tramèr's stated aim is to 'understand and mitigate long-term threats to the safety and privacy of users' by studying models' worst-case behaviour adversarially, arguing that many proposed defences give a false sense of security unless evaluated against adaptive attackers. His current research focuses on how AI agents introduce new security and privacy risks, and he aims for findings to inform both technical and legislative protections. No AGI timeline or p(doom) from him was found.

background: Gillian Kereldena Hadfield (born July 14, 1961) is a Canadian economist, legal scholar and artificial intelligence researcher who is the Bloomberg Distinguished Professor of AI Alignment and Governance. She is also Professor of Law and of Strategic Management at Toronto, Canada CIFAR AI Chair at the Vector Institute, and an AI2050 Senior Fellow. From 2018 to 2023, Hadfield served as Senior Policy Adviser to the artificial intelligence company OpenAI.

She was previously the director and eponymous chair of the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society and professor in the Faculty of Law at the University of Toronto, and the Richard L. and Antoinette Schamoi Kirtland Professor of Law and Professor of Economics at the University of Southern California. At USC, Hadfield directed the Southern California Innovation Project and the USC Center in Law, Economics, and Organization. She is a former member of the board of directors for the American Law and Economics Association and the International Society for New Institutional Economics.

p: Hadfield received her BA with honours in economics from Queen's University in 1983. She earned a JD with distinction from Stanford Law School in 1988 and a PhD in economics from Stanford University in 1990.
Following law school, Hadfield clerked for Judge Patricia M. Wald of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

Hadfield joined the faculty of the UC Berkeley School of Law as an assistant law professor in 1990. From 1994 to 1999, Hadfield was an associate law professor at the University of Toronto Faculty of Law, and then a professor of law from 1999 to 2001. Hadfield also served as a professor with NYU School of Law's Global Law Faculty from 1999 to 2001.

Hadfield moved to the USC Gould School of Law in 2001, where she was appointed the Richard L. and Antoinette Schamoi Kirtland Professor of Law and Professor of Economics at the University of Southern California, serving in the role to 2018.

In 2016, she was the Daniel R. Fischel and Sylvia M. Neil Distinguished visiting professor of Law at the University of Chicago Law School. In 2010, Hadfield was the Sidley Austin Visiting Professor at Harvard Law School, and in 2008, was the Justin W. D'Atri Visiting Professor of Law, Business, and Society at Columbia Law School. In 2006–2007 and 2010–2011, Hadfield served as a fellow of the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University, and in 1993, served as a National Fellow at the Hoover Institution.

employers: Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society

background: Gregory (Greg) Wayne is an American neuroscientist and AI researcher. He received a B.S. in Symbolic Systems from Stanford University, an M.S. in Applied Mathematics from the City University of New York, and a PhD in Neuroscience from Columbia University (2007–2013), working in Larry Abbott's theoretical neuroscience laboratory; he also attended and later taught at the Marine Biological Laboratory's Methods in Computational Neuroscience course.

He joined DeepMind in London around 2013–2014, shortly after its acquisition by Google, and has worked there since, now holding the title of Distinguished Scientist at Google DeepMind. With Alex Graves and Ivo Danihelka he co-authored 'Neural Turing Machines' (2014), which coupled neural networks to an external, differentiable memory, and its successor, the Differentiable Neural Computer ('Hybrid computing using a neural network with dynamic external memory', Nature 2016). His later research spanned memory-based reinforcement learning — including MERLIN (Memory, RL and Inference Network, 2018) — grid-cell-like representations for navigation in artificial agents (Nature 2018), humanoid motor control, long-term credit assignment, and embodied language use in virtual robots, as well as the influential perspective 'A deep learning framework for neuroscience' (Nature Neuroscience 2019) and 'Toward an Integration of Deep Learning and Neuroscience' (2016).

MIT Technology Review named him one of its 35 Innovators Under 35 in 2017 for 'using an understanding of the brain to create smarter machines'. Since 2021 he has led Google's Project Astra, the multimodal dialogue research programme aimed at building a universal AI assistant, and he advises Protocol Labs R&D on neuroscience.

background: Gretchen Krueger is an American AI policy researcher. She earned a BA from Harvard University and an MA from Columbia University, and is also trained as a lawyer. Before AI work she was at the New York City Economic Development Corporation, then a research assistant/program associate at NYU's AI Now Institute (2018–2019), contributing to the AI Now 2018 Report.

She joined OpenAI's Policy Research team in 2019, focusing on accountability in AI development and on the risks and limitations of new systems. She co-authored 'Release Strategies and the Social Impacts of Language Models' (2019, on GPT-2's staged release), the GPT-3 paper 'Language Models are Few-Shot Learners' (NeurIPS 2020 Outstanding Paper), 'Toward Trustworthy AI Development: Mechanisms for Supporting Verifiable Claims' (2020), and risk analyses for CLIP, DALL·E, Codex ('Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code', hazards section) and the GPT-4 Technical Report and system card (2023).

Krueger resigned from OpenAI on 14 May 2024, hours before Ilya Sutskever and Jan Leike announced their departures, and said on 22 May that she shared their concerns and had 'additional and overlapping concerns'. From 2024 to 2025 she was a fellow at Harvard's Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society, where she remains an affiliate and independent researcher, and since November 2025 she has volunteered with Evitable, a group that challenges the idea that AGI is inevitable.

gretchen-krueger.views: On leaving OpenAI in May 2024 Krueger wrote: 'We need to do more to improve foundational things like decision-making processes; accountability; transparency; documentation; policy enforcement; the care with which we use our own technology; and mitigations for impacts on inequality, rights, and the environment,' adding that these concerns influence 'how aspects of the future can be charted, and by whom', and suggested tech companies can disempower critics by sowing division. According to her Berkman Klein profile she 'has long challenged the assumption that A(G)I is inevitable' and now focuses on supporting those resisting the race to develop and drive adoption of ever more powerful AI. No numerical forecasts found.

background: Hiroaki Kitano (北野 宏明; born 1961 in Tokyo) is a Japanese scientist, head of the Systems Biology Institute, Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Technology Officer of the Sony Group Corporation, Chief Executive Officer of Sony Research Inc. and Sony Computer Science Laboratories, Inc.; a Group Director of the Laboratory for Disease Systems Modeling at and RIKEN Center for Integrative Medical Sciences; and a professor at Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST). Kitano is known for developing AIBO, and the robotic world cup tournament known as Robocup.

p: Kitano graduated from International Christian University with a B.A. in physics in 1984. He received a PhD in computer science from Kyoto University in 1991. His PhD thesis in machine translation was titled "Speech-to-speech translation: a massively parallel memory-based approach".  His work includes a broad spectrum of publications in artificial intelligence and interactomics.
From 1988 to 1994, Kitano was a visiting researcher at the Center for Machine Translation at Carnegie Mellon University.

At Sony, Kitano started the development of the AIBO robotic pet. This research was developed further as the QRIO, a bipedal humanoid robot. The research behind AIBO and QRIO led to Kitano founding the RoboCup annual international robotics competition in 1997. The goal of RoboCup is to create a team of autonomous robotic footballers that would be able to beat the best team in the world, by 2050.
Kitano has made significant contributions to Systems biology, including a contribution to the Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML).

Kitano has served as a scientific advisor for a number of companies, including Alstom, Segway Japan and Mitsubishi Chemical Holdings. He was awarded the IJCAI Computers and Thought Award in 1993 and the Nature Award for Creative Mentoring in Science in 2009. He was elected a Fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence in 2021.

predictions.claim: Develop AI Scientists capable of autonomously carrying out research to make major scientific discoveries worthy of Nobel Prize and beyond by 2050 (Nobel Turing Challenge).
predictions.evidence: AI-driven work already won a Nobel: the 2024 Chemistry prize went to Hassabis and Jumper for AlphaFold2 (2020), which solved a 50-year protein-structure problem - but the laureates are humans, not an autonomous AI scientist.

background: Holger H. Hoos is a German-Canadian computer scientist and a Alexander von Humboldt-professor of artificial intelligence at RWTH Aachen University. He also holds a part-time appointment as a professor of machine learning at Leiden University, and he is an adjunct professor at the Computer Science Department of the University of British Columbia, where he held a full-time professorial appointment from 2000 until 2016. His research interests are focused on artificial intelligence, at the intersection of machine learning, automated reasoning and optimization, with applications in empirical algorithmics, bioinformatics and operations research.

In particular, he works on automated algorithm design and on stochastic local search algorithms. Since 2015, he is a Fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI), and since 2020 a Fellow of the European Association for Artificial Intelligence (EurAI) as well as a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM).

He wrote the book Stochastic Local Search: Foundations and Applications (with Thomas Stützle), and his research is published widely in internationally leading journals and conference proceedings. In 2023 he received the ACM SIGKDD test-of-time award for his work on Auto-WEKA, together with Chris Thornton, Frank Hutter and Kevin Leyton-Brown. He also works in computer music, where he created the SALIERI music programming language and computer music system (with Thomas Helbich, Jürgen Kilian and Kai Renz) as well as GUIDO music notation (with Keith Hamel).
Hoos studied computer science at Department of Computer Science of the Technische Universität Darmstadt and received his doctorate there in 1998.

Ian J. Goodfellow (born 1987) is an American computer scientist, engineer, and executive, most noted for his work on artificial neural networks and deep learning. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind, was previously employed as a research scientist at Google Brain, and director of machine learning at Apple, as well as one of the first employees at OpenAI. He has made several important contributions to the field of deep learning, including the invention of the generative adversarial network (GAN). Goodfellow co-wrote, as the first author, the textbook Deep Learning (2016) and wrote the chapter on deep learning in the authoritative textbook of the field of artificial intelligence, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (used in more than 1,500 universities in 135 countries).

p: Goodfellow obtained his BSc and MSc in computer science from Stanford University under the supervision of Andrew Ng, and his PhD in machine learning from the Université de Montréal in February 2015, under the supervision of Yoshua Bengio and Aaron Courville. Goodfellow's thesis is titled Deep learning of representations and its application to computer vision.

After graduation, Goodfellow joined Google as part of the Google Brain research team. In March 2016, he left Google to join the newly founded OpenAI research laboratory. 11 months later, in March 2017, Goodfellow returned to Google Research, but left again in 2019.

In 2019, Goodfellow joined Apple as director of machine learning in the Special Projects Group. He resigned from Apple in April 2022 to protest Apple's plan to require in-person work for its employees. Shortly after, Goodfellow then joined Google DeepMind as a research scientist.

Goodfellow is best known for inventing generative adversarial networks (GANs), using deep learning to generate images. This approach uses two neural networks to competitively  improve an image's quality. A “generator” network creates a synthetic image based on an initial set of images such as a collection of faces. A “discriminator” network tries to determine whether images are authentic or created by the generator. The generate-detect cycle is repeated. For each iteration, the generator and the discriminator use the other's feedback to improve or detect the generated images, until the discriminator can no longer distinguish between generated and authentic images. However, GANs have also been used to create deepfakes.

At Google, Goodfellow developed a system enabling Google Maps to automatically transcribe addresses from photos taken by Street View cars and demonstrated security vulnerabilities of machine learning systems.

background: Jakub Pachocki (born 1991) is a Polish computer scientist and former competitive programmer. He is best known as OpenAI's chief scientist and for his role in overseeing development of GPT-4.

p: After graduation, Pachocki did postdoctoral work at Harvard University and the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing.

In 2017, Pachocki joined OpenAI. In 2021, he became OpenAI's research director where he led the development of  GPT-4 and OpenAI Five. In May 2024, he became chief scientist after his mentor Ilya Sutskever left the company. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has called Pachocki "easily one of the greatest minds of our generation".

In September 2026, Pachocki published an essay entitled An Alien Mind in which he discusses the rapid advancement of AI systems and the ongoing challenge of ensuring they remain aligned with human goals. He also called for the establishment of shared safety regulations and an international cooperation regarding the development of the AI technology.

background: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein is an American machine-learning researcher working across AI, physics, neuroscience and dynamical systems. He earned BAs in Physics and (through the College Scholar program) quantum computing from Cornell University in 2001, then worked from 2001 to 2005 as a research associate on NASA JPL's Mars Exploration Rovers mission, including on the Pancam cameras of Spirit and Opportunity. He completed a PhD in Biophysics at UC Berkeley in 2012 in Bruno Olshausen's lab at the Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience.

From 2012 to 2015 he was a visiting scholar in Surya Ganguli's lab at Stanford (and an academic resident at Khan Academy, modelling student learning). There he wrote 'Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics' (ICML 2015), which introduced diffusion models — the basis of modern image generators such as DALL·E and Stable Diffusion. He joined Google Brain in 2015, rising from senior research scientist to principal scientist at Google DeepMind (2023–2024). There he co-authored 'Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations' (ICLR 2021 Outstanding Paper), led work on learned optimizers, infinite-width network theory (Neural Tangents), co-led the BIG-bench language-model benchmark, and co-authored 'Levels of AGI' (2023).

In February 2024 he joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff. He also writes a blog of unusual ideas, including 'The hot mess theory of AI misalignment' (2023) and a viral study showing that the boundary of neural-network trainability is fractal, and makes generative art.

jascha-sohl-dickstein.views: In his 2023 'hot mess theory of AI misalignment' Sohl-Dickstein argued that an AI could be misaligned either by 'monomaniacally' pursuing the wrong goal (supercoherence) or by acting incoherently, and presented evidence that more intelligent entities tend to behave less coherently — suggesting incoherent failures deserve more weight relative to classic single-goal takeover scenarios. He has argued that we should worry about 'a *diversity* of risks', since focusing only on present harms or only on AGI misalignment would leave us overwhelmed by other forms of AI-enabled disruption, and that aligning systems built out of many AIs is to AI alignment 'what good governance is to raising an ethical human'. He co-authored the 'Levels of AGI' framework for measuring progress and risk. No numerical timeline or p(doom) found.

background: Jasjeet "Jas" Singh Sekhon is a data scientist, political scientist, and statistician at Yale University. Sekhon is the Eugene Meyer Professor at Yale University, a fellow of the American Statistical Association, and a fellow of the Society for Political Methodology. Sekhon's primary research interests lie in causal inference, machine learning, and their intersection. He has also published research on their application in various fields including voting behavior, online experimentation, epidemiology, and medicine.

p: Sekhon graduated with a B.A. from the University of British Columbia. In 1999, he earned a Ph.D. at Cornell University.

Sekhon's career in academia began in 1999, when he became an assistant professor at Harvard University. He stayed at Harvard until 2005 when he moved to UC Berkeley. At Berkeley, he was appointed as the Robson Professor of Political Science and Statistics in 2014. In 2018, he accepted a non-academic position at Bridgewater Associates, where he was chief scientist and head of AI/ML. In 2020, he left Berkeley to join Yale University, where he was appointed Meyer Professor of Political Science and Statistics and Data Science in 2021. He was named a fellow of the Society for Political Methodology in 2019 and a fellow of the American Statistical Association in 2021. In March 2026, Sekhon joined Google DeepMind as its chief strategy officer after leaving his executive role at Bridgewater, while also joining its board.

Sekhon has authored or co-authored dozens of journal articles and several widely used software packages. The topics of his scholarship include experimental research methods, machine learning for estimating causal effects, election fraud, and matching. His research has been widely cited.

Sekhon is best known for his research in causal inference and machine learning. His early research on causal inference focused on the role of matching, but he later wrote an article pointing out that matching is unable to address many of the problems (particularly the selection on observables assumption) that its proponents assume. Nevertheless, his Genetic Matching algorithm remains one of his most highly cited articles. As of 2021, his research focuses on developing interpretable and credible machine learning methods for estimating causal relationships.

One of Sekhon's first publications, a journal article in Digestive Diseases and Sciences, presented a novel treatment, glucocorticoid, for a rare disease that he suffered. Sekhon himself was the first case described in the article.

awards: Fellow of the American Statistical Association (2021)

background: Jeffrey Adgate Dean (born July 23, 1968) is an American computer scientist and software engineer. He is best known for his work at Google, which he joined in 1999. He led Google AI from 2018 to 2023 and was Google's chief scientist from 2023 to 2026.  Dean co-founded the AI research start-up Discovery Loop in 2026.

p: Dean received a B.S., summa cum laude, from the University of Minnesota in computer science and economics in 1990. His undergraduate thesis was on neural networks in C programming, advised by Vipin Kumar.

He received a Ph.D. in computer science from the department that would become the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of Washington in 1996, working under Craig Chambers on compilers and whole-program optimization techniques for object-oriented programming languages. He was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2009, which recognized his work on "the science and engineering of large-scale distributed computer systems".

Before joining Google, Dean worked at DEC/Compaq's Western Research Laboratory, where he worked on profiling tools, microprocessor architecture and information retrieval. Much of his work was completed in close collaboration with Sanjay Ghemawat.
Before graduate school, he worked at the World Health Organization's Global Programme on AIDS, developing software for statistical modeling and forecasting of the HIV/AIDS pandemic.

Dean joined Google in mid-1999. He joined Google X in 2011 to investigate deep neural networks, which had just resurged in popularity. This ended with "the cat neuron paper", a deep belief network trained by unsupervised learning on YouTube videos. This project morphed into Google Brain, also formed in 2011. Jeff Dean became its leader in 2012. In April 2018, he was appointed the head of Google's artificial intelligence division, after John Giannandrea left to lead Apple's AI projects. As of 2018, Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat were the only two employees at Google to hold the title of Senior Fellow, the highest technical level at the company.

He is the subject of an Internet meme for "Jeff Dean facts". Similar to Chuck Norris facts, the Jeff Dean facts exaggerate his programming powers. For example:Once, in early 2002, when the index servers went down, Jeff Dean answered user queries manually for two hours. Evals showed a quality improvement of 5 points.

background: Jerry (Jarosław) Tworek is a Polish AI researcher and entrepreneur. He earned a master's degree in (applied) mathematics from the University of Warsaw and interned at J.P. Morgan (2012–2013) before spending about five years as a quantitative trader/researcher in Amsterdam, developing futures-trading strategies using optimisation and signal-extraction techniques — work that drew him to reinforcement learning.

He joined OpenAI in 2019 as a research scientist working on neural program synthesis and reinforcement learning. He co-authored 'Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand' (2019) and was second author of 'Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code' (2021), which introduced Codex, the model behind the original GitHub Copilot. He contributed to GPT-4 and ChatGPT (including code interpreter and plugins), and was the overall leadership lead for OpenAI o1 (September 2024), the first of OpenAI's reinforcement-learning-trained reasoning models, later contributing to o3 and the reasoning in GPT-5. He became a vice president of research (described as VP of RL).

In January 2026, after nearly seven years, Tworek left OpenAI to pursue research he said was hard to do there, arguing that big labs are locked into scaling transformers via pre-training and RL. In April 2026 he launched Core Automation in San Francisco as co-founder and CEO, aiming to build 'the most automated AI lab in the world' by automating its own research and developing new learning algorithms and architectures that go beyond pre-training, RL and transformers, with a focus on continual learning.

background: Jess Whittlestone is a British AI policy researcher. She earned a first-class degree (master's) in Mathematics and Philosophy from the University of Oxford and a PhD in Behavioural Science from Warwick Business School, University of Warwick (2013–2017), with a thesis arguing that confirmation is not necessarily a bias, supervised by Nick Chater. She then worked for the Behavioural Insights Team advising UK government departments on data, evidence and evaluation, and as a freelance research consultant for the Centre for Effective Altruism (2017).

In February 2018 she joined the University of Cambridge as a postdoctoral researcher in AI policy at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence (CFI) and the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER), becoming a Senior Research Fellow/Associate (2020) and Deputy Director of the AI: Futures and Responsibility programme. She published peer-reviewed work on AI ethics and governance, including 'The Role and Limits of Principles in AI Ethics: Towards a Focus on Tensions' (2019), led a project informing the Ada Lovelace Institute's strategy, and co-authored the 2021 report 'Future Proof: The Opportunity to Transform the UK's Resilience to Extreme Risks' with Toby Ord and others.

In March 2022 she joined the Centre for Long-Term Resilience (CLTR), a UK think tank on extreme risks, as its first Head of AI Policy, leading its AI policy recommendations and advocacy to UK government — including evidence to the UK Future of Compute Review recommending compute monitoring and governance, and co-authoring 'Model evaluation for extreme risks' (2023) and the Alan Turing Institute/CETaS guide 'Strengthening Resilience to AI Risk' (2023). She later became CLTR's Senior Advisor on AI Policy, and is a member of the CNAS AI Governance Forum.

She has argued that high-level AI ethics principles are a starting point but too broad to guide action, so attention should go to the tensions between them; at CLTR she advocates concrete UK policy to reduce extreme risks from AI, such as government monitoring and governance of compute, rigorous model evaluations for dangerous capabilities, and building societal resilience to AI risk. background: Jonas Geiping is a German machine-learning researcher. He holds bachelor's and master's degrees in mathematics from the University of Münster (WWU) and received his PhD (Dr. rer. nat.) in computer science from the University of Siegen in 2021, advised by Michael Möller, working on optimisation in computer vision and machine-learning security. From September 2021 to October 2023 he was a postdoctoral researcher with Tom Goldstein at the University of Maryland, College Park, researching privacy, security and efficiency.

His earlier work showed that gradients shared in federated learning can leak private training data ('Inverting Gradients', NeurIPS 2020) and that data poisoning against industrial-scale image classifiers such as Google Cloud AutoML is feasible ('Witches' Brew', ICLR 2021). He co-authored 'A Watermark for Large Language Models' (ICML 2023 Outstanding Paper), which was covered by the New York Times and Nature, quoted in US Congressional testimony and anticipates text-watermarking requirements in the EU AI Act. He also showed language models can be coerced into adversarial behaviours beyond jailbreaking, studied baseline defences against LLM attacks, explored training under tight compute budgets ('Cramming', ICML 2023), and developed latent reasoning via depth-recurrent models (2025).

In October 2023 he moved to Tübingen, where he leads the Safety- and Efficiency-aligned Learning (SEAL) group jointly at the ELLIS Institute Tübingen (as a Hector Endowed ELLIS Fellow) and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, and is a faculty member and steering-committee member of the Tübingen AI Center. He received the DAGM German Pattern Recognition Award in 2025, was Experiment Chair of NeurIPS 2025, has contributed to red-teaming for major AI providers, and taught AI safety at the University of Tübingen in 2026.

jonas-geiping.views: Geiping describes his aim as understanding 'how to construct safe intelligent systems', an approach he calls 'constructive AI safety': beyond passively evaluating frontier models, asking how models or systems could be designed differently so that 'intelligence and safety reinforce each other', and finding 'feasible technical solutions that reduce harm without hamstringing artificial systems'. He has asked publicly whether models can ever be made 'safe' and how that should be defined. No AGI timeline or p(doom) found.

background: Joshua (Josh) Achiam is an American AI safety researcher and futurist. He earned B.S. degrees in Aerospace Engineering and Physics from the University of Florida (2014) and a PhD in Electrical Engineering and Computer Sciences from UC Berkeley (2021), advised by Pieter Abbeel and Shankar Sastry, with a dissertation on 'Exploration and Safety in Deep Reinforcement Learning'. His early research included Constrained Policy Optimization (ICML 2017), a method for training RL agents that respect safety constraints, and safe-exploration benchmarks.

He joined OpenAI in 2017 (research scientist from December 2017) on the safety team, working on safe RL, AI safety research and operations and AI impacts research. He created Spinning Up in Deep RL (2018), a widely used educational resource, and co-authored 'On First-Order Meta-Learning Algorithms' (Reptile, 2018), 'Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code' (Codex, 2021), the GPT-4 technical report (2023) and the GPT-4o system card (2024). In September 2024 he became OpenAI's Head of Mission Alignment, tasked with defining and communicating OpenAI's mission that AGI benefit all of humanity, and in February 2026 he became OpenAI's Chief Futurist, studying how the world will change in response to AI and AGI, alongside former national-labs physicist Jason Pruet.

Achiam left OpenAI in July 2026 to work independently. From October 2026 he is a non-resident senior fellow at both the Institute for Progress and the Foundation for American Innovation, focusing on how rapid AI progress creates new public-policy and national-security needs, and on 21 October 2026 he testified to a California State Senate hearing on AI development timelines and risks. (Note: the source record lists him as a researcher at OpenAI; he left in July 2026.)

josh-achiam.views: In October 2026 testimony to the California Senate, Achiam said today's frontier models 'are probably already superintelligent in some interesting ways', that the field's consensus is that progress is accelerating, and that the field considers recursive self-improvement 'a near-term (next 2 years) phenomenon'. He laid out a scenario in which 'in 2028, extremely capable AI arrives in most domains', 'by 2030, AI diffuses and significantly accelerates all knowledge work', and 'by 2035, robots plausibly accelerate all physical work', while the social fabric strains, 'rogue AI becomes a real issue' and national security foundations are affected — 'every disruption, everywhere, all at once', arriving amid a crisis of trust. He recommended standards and licensing for professional AI use, safety-information management requirements, public compute to support enforcement and cyber resilience, using AI to lower the cost of living, and funding university AI safety research. He has said his goal is 'to ensure that the long-term future of humanity is good'.

background: Joshua Batson is an American mathematician and interpretability researcher. He earned a BA in Mathematics from Yale University, a Master of Advanced Study (Part III) in Mathematics from the University of Cambridge (2009) and a PhD in Mathematics from MIT (2014), working in low-dimensional and quantum topology. After his PhD he worked on quantitative problems across fields: a WIRED science-writing fellowship (2014), computer-vision and machine-learning consulting (including cybersecurity at Sift Security, 2015–2016).

From 2017 to 2021 he was a senior research scientist at the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub in San Francisco, working on viral genomics, metagenomics and computational microscopy. He co-developed Noise2Self, a self-supervised method for blind denoising (2019), and contributed to the Tabula Muris single-cell atlas of mouse organs and a single-mosquito sequencing study. During COVID-19 his team stood up a high-throughput CLIA PCR testing lab in San Francisco in eight days, and he co-led the COVID Tracker project bringing genomic sequencing and variant analysis to about a dozen California counties covering more than five million people. He later served as chief data scientist at a public-health organisation.

He joined Anthropic as a research scientist in March 2023. He was a co-first author of 'Towards Monosemanticity' (2023), co-authored 'Scaling Monosemanticity' (2024), and leads the circuits effort of Anthropic's mechanistic-interpretability team, serving as corresponding author of 'Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models' and 'On the Biology of a Large Language Model' (March 2025), which used attribution graphs as an 'AI microscope' to trace how Claude 3.5 Haiku plans rhymes, does arithmetic and performs multi-step reasoning. He also co-authored 'Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability' (2025) and 'Auditing language models for hidden objectives' (2025).

background: Julian Schrittwieser is an Austrian AI researcher who grew up in a village in the Austrian countryside and taught himself programming by writing games. He studied software engineering at the Vienna University of Technology (TU Wien, BSc 2013); after a summer internship at Google following his first year, he joined Google full-time in 2013 while finishing his degree and moved to London, initially working on advertising infrastructure.

After hearing a talk by Demis Hassabis he moved to DeepMind around 2014, joining the AlphaGo team as one of its three original developers. He worked on AlphaGo (2016), was second author of AlphaGo Zero (2017), co-authored AlphaZero (2018), and was first author of MuZero ('Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model', Nature 2020), which plans using a learned world model. He rose from senior software engineer to staff software engineer (2018) and principal research engineer (2021), contributing to OpenSpiel, AlphaCode, AlphaTensor (faster matrix multiplication), Gumbel MuZero, MuZero rate control for YouTube video compression, and AlphaProof, the RL agent for olympiad-level formal mathematics (IMO 2024 silver-medal standard; Nature paper 2025).

In October 2024 he joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff working on reasoning, planning and search, saying Anthropic is the company he most trusts to build AGI safely. His September 2025 blog post 'Failing to Understand the Exponential, Again', comparing AI-bubble talk to early-COVID complacency, went viral; he followed it with a June 2026 post, 'The New Left Behind', on AI skeptics.

julian-schrittwieser.views: Schrittwieser argues that people struggle to intuit exponential trends: since AI's autonomous task length doubles roughly every 3–4 months with no slowdown visible inside frontier labs, frontier-lab valuations are 'fairly conservative', though parts of the wider AI ecosystem may be a bubble. He says simply extrapolating straight lines (e.g., METR time horizons, GDPval) beats most experts, and believes pre-training + RL + transformers will very likely reach roughly human-level performance on economically relevant tasks. He considers a true discontinuous takeoff 'extremely unlikely', expecting visible warning signs and the option to pause, sees pre-training on human data as helpful for alignment because it imparts human-like values, and expects AI to complement rather than replace workers one-for-one, with distribution of gains being a political problem.
