background: Ricardo A. Baeza-Yates (born March 21, 1961) is a Chilean computer scientist specializing in algorithms, data structures, information retrieval, web search and responsible AI. Since 2025 he is a part-time Wallenberg AI, Autonomous Systems and Software Program professor at the KTH Royal Institute of Technology of Sweden in Stockholm. He is also part-time professor at Universitat Pompeu Fabra in Barcelona and Universidad de Chile in Santiago. He is an expert member of the Global Partnership on Artificial Intelligence, a member of the Association for Computing Machinery's US Technology Policy Committee as well as IEEE's AI Committee.

He is member of the Chilean Academy of Sciences (2002), founding member of the Chilean Academy of Engineering (2010), corresponding member of the Brazilian Academy of Sciences (2018), and member of the Academia Europaea (2023).
He is an ACM Fellow (2009). and an IEEE Fellow (2011). He is a former member of Spain's Advisory Council on AI (2019–2023).
From January 2021 to March 2025 he was the Director of Research at the Institute for Experiential AI at Northeastern University in the Silicon Valley campus.

From June 2016 until June 2020 he was CTO of NTENT, a semantic search technology company. Before, from January 2006 until February 2016, he was VP of Research for Yahoo! Labs, leading teams in United States, Europe, Asia and Latin America.

p: He obtained a PhD from the University of Waterloo with Efficient Text Searching, supervised by Gaston Gonnet and granted in 1989.

Algorithms and data structures. His contributions include algorithms for string search such as the Shift Or Algorithm and algorithms for Fuzzy string searching, inspiring also the Bitap algorithm; co-author of the Handbook of Algorithms and Data Structures (ISBN 0-201-14218-X) with his former PhD advisor Gaston Gonnet,

Information retrieval. Co-author of Modern Information retrieval Addison Wesley (ISBN 0-201-39829-X), first edition in 1999 and a second edition in 2011 that won the 2012 book of the year award of the  Association for Information Science and Technology.

Web search and mining. Baeza-Yates founded in 2002 and directed until 2005 the Center for Web Research in the Department of Computer Science of the University of Chile. His latest work on this area focuses on bias on the Web, giving the Gödel Lecture 2017 in Viena.

awards: Salvà and Campillo award for outstanding person (2019)

background: Richard Stuart Sutton  (born 1957 or 1958) is an American-Canadian computer scientist. He is a professor of computing science at the University of Alberta and chief scientific advisor at the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute. In 2024, Sutton received the Turing Award alongside his supervisor Andrew Barto for their work in reinforcement learning.

Sutton is considered one of the founders of modern computational reinforcement learning, known for his contributions to temporal difference learning and policy gradient methods. He proposed the "bitter lesson", an influential observation about AI scaling limits. He is on the scientific advisory committee of the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society.

p: Richard Sutton was born in either 1957 or 1958 in Toledo, Ohio, and grew up in Oak Brook, Illinois, a suburb of Chicago, United States.

Sutton received his Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree in psychology from Stanford University in 1978 before taking a Master of Science (1980) and PhD (1984) in computer science from the University of Massachusetts Amherst supervised by Andrew Barto. His doctoral dissertation introduced actor-critic architectures and temporal credit assignment.

He was influenced by Harry Klopf's work in the 1970s, which proposed that supervised learning is insufficient for AI or explaining intelligent behavior, and trial-and-error learning, driven by "hedonic aspects of behavior", is necessary. This focused his interest to reinforcement learning.

Sutton held a postdoctoral research position at the University of Massachusetts Amherst in 1984. He worked at GTE Laboratories in Waltham, Massachusetts as principal member of technical staff from 1985 to 1994, then returned to the University of Massachusetts Amherst as a senior research scientist. He joined AT&T Labs Shannon Laboratory in Florham Park, New Jersey as principal technical staff member from 1998 to 2002. He has been a professor of computing science at the University of Alberta since 2003, where he helped establish the Reinforcement Learning and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory.

From 2017 to 2023, he worked at Google DeepMind as a distinguished research scientist. He helped launch DeepMind Alberta in Edmonton, a research office operated in close collaboration with the University of Alberta. Following that, he joined Keen Technologies, John Carmack's AI research company. In 2026, he left Keen Technologies alongside Khurram Javed to launch Oak Lab, an AI startup aiming to develop AI agents that can continually learn from their environment through reinforcement learning.

Sutton has been a fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI) since 2001; his nomination read: "For significant contributions to many topics in machine learning, including reinforcement learning, temporal difference techniques, and neural networks."  In 2003, he received the President's Award from the International Neural Network Society and in 2013, the Outstanding Achievement in Research award from the University of Massachusetts Amherst. In 2021, he was appointed Canada CIFAR AI Chair and received the IJCAI Award for Research Excellence. He received the 2024 Turing Award from the Association for Computing Machinery together with Andrew Barto; the citation of the award read: "For developing the conceptual and algorithmic foundations of reinforcement learning."
In 2016, Sutton was elected Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada. In 2021, he was elected Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) of London.

Sutton introduced temporal-difference methods for prediction and control, establishing convergence properties and practical algorithms. He proposed integrated learning and planning through the Dyna architecture. He co-developed the options framework for temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning. He co-authored the first modern policy gradient formulation with function approximation.
Sutton's essay The Bitter Lesson argued that general methods that scale with computation dominate domain-specific approaches in the long run.
His former doctoral students include David Silver and Doina Precup.
Sutton became a Canadian citizen in 2015, and his renunciation of US citizenship was reported in 2017.

awards: Lifetime Achievement Award of the Canadian Artificial Intelligence Association (2018)

background: Robert F. Trager is a political scientist who specialises in international relations and the international governance of AI and other emerging technologies. He earned a BA in philosophy from Middlebury College (1995) and an MSc from the London School of Economics (1997), and worked in the investment banking division of Lehman Brothers in New York before doctoral study at Columbia University (MPhil 2002, PhD in political science 2007).

He taught at Oxford, held an Olin Fellowship at Harvard and a faculty position at Yale, and then joined UCLA, where he became Professor of Political Science; from 2017 to 2021 he was Assistant Director for Research of UCLA's Burkle Center for International Relations. His earlier research asked how states form beliefs about each other's intentions, the role of diplomacy and costly signals, coercion and international terrorism, published in the American Political Science Review, International Organization and International Security; his book 'Diplomacy: Communication and the Origins of International Order' (Cambridge University Press, 2017) grew out of this work. He has written two books in all.

He moved to the University of Oxford, where he is Co-Director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative (AIGI), Senior Research Fellow at the Blavatnik School of Government, and International Governance Lead at the Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI). His AI work covers frontier AI regulation, jurisdictional certification for civilian AI, compute governance, AI safety as a global public good and the design of a UN scientific panel on AI. He has advised governments and industry, spoke at the AI Seoul Summit (2024) in favour of international reporting on AI developers and compute providers, and moderated AI Governance Day at the 2024 AI for Good summit in Geneva.

robert-trager.views: Trager argues that AI risk calls for international institutions, drawing on lessons from nuclear and other technology regimes. He has proposed international certification of jurisdictions that regulate civilian AI, licensing and oversight of frontier models, and, at the 2024 AI Seoul Summit, international reporting requirements for AI developers and compute providers. He treats AI safety as a global public good that needs cooperation between rival states, and has argued that a UN scientific panel on AI must balance rigour with legitimacy. No personal AGI timeline or p(doom) figure was found.

background: Roger Baker Grosse is a machine-learning researcher known for work on neural-network optimisation and training dynamics, now focused on AI alignment. He studied at Stanford, earning a BS in Symbolic Systems with honors (2007) and an MS in Computer Science (2008) while doing research with Andrew Ng. He completed a PhD in EECS at MIT in 2014 under William Freeman (also working with Josh Tenenbaum), with the thesis 'Model selection in compositional spaces', which included early automatic model-structure search; he won the best student paper award at UAI 2012.

He was a postdoc at the University of Toronto (2014–2016, with an NSERC Banting fellowship), became an assistant professor there in 2016 and associate professor in 2022, and was a founding member of the Vector Institute, holding a Canada CIFAR AI Chair since 2017. His group worked on second-order optimisation (K-FAC, with James Martens), Bayesian deep learning and uncertainty, hyperparameter tuning, and influence functions. He was a member of the Institute for Advanced Study in early 2020 and has held a Sloan Fellowship, a Canada Research Chair and the Schwartz Reisman Chair in Technology and Society.

Since July 2022 he has also been a Member of Technical Staff on Anthropic's Alignment Science team, where his work focuses on training-data attribution; he led Anthropic's 2023 study 'Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions'. He holds a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Senior Fellowship and gives talks on topics such as 'How can deep learning research inform long-term AI safety?' (2021) and 'On the origin of rogue AI' (2024).

roger-grosse.views: Grosse writes that 'given how fast AI is progressing, the problem of ensuring AIs are robustly aligned with human values seems like the most important thing we can be working on now'. He has shifted his research from optimisation to applying an understanding of deep learning to alignment, and argues that empirical study, such as influence functions that trace behaviour back to training data, can turn risk pathways for rogue AI that were once 'philosophical thought experiments' into things that can be studied. No numeric AGI timeline or p(doom) figure from him was found.

background: Ross Brook Girshick is a computer-vision researcher best known for bringing deep learning to object detection. He completed his PhD in computer science at the University of Chicago in 2012 under Pedro Felzenszwalb, with the dissertation 'From Rigid Templates to Grammars: Object Detection with Structured Models'. During his PhD he interned at Microsoft Research Cambridge (UK) on human pose estimation from depth images, contributed to top PASCAL VOC detection entries, and received the PASCAL VOC 'lifetime achievement' prize in 2010 for work on deformable part models.

From 2012 to 2014 he was a postdoctoral fellow at UC Berkeley with Jitendra Malik and Trevor Darrell, where in 2013 he created R-CNN ('Regions with CNN features'). He then worked as a researcher at Microsoft Research in Redmond (2014–2015), where he developed Fast R-CNN and co-authored Faster R-CNN and YOLO, and as a research scientist at Facebook AI Research / Meta (2015–2023), where he co-authored Mask R-CNN, Feature Pyramid Networks, focal loss (RetinaNet), Masked Autoencoders and Segment Anything, and wrote the open-source Detectron platform.

He joined the Allen Institute for AI's PRIOR team at the end of 2023, co-authoring the open vision-language models Molmo and PixMo (2024). In late 2024 he co-founded Vercept, a startup whose product Vy uses computer vision to let AI agents operate any application. Anthropic acquired Vercept in February 2026, and Girshick joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff working on Claude's computer-use abilities. His honours include the PAMI Young Researcher Award (2017), three PAMI Mark Everingham Prizes (2017, 2021, 2023) and test-of-time awards including the 2024 Longuet-Higgins Prize for R-CNN; his work has hundreds of thousands of citations.

background: Rumman Chowdhury (b. April 1980) is a Bangladeshi American data scientist, a business founder, and former responsible artificial intelligence lead at Accenture. She was born in Rockland County, New York. She is recognized for her contributions to the field of data science.

Chowdhury's engagement with science was motivated by her enthusiasm for science fiction, a passion that stimulated her curiosity, often attributed to the "Dana Scully Effect." According to Chowdhury, this laid the foundation for her future endeavors.

p: Chowdhury completed her undergraduate study in Management Science and Political Science at Massachusetts Institute of Technology. She received a Master of Science from Columbia University in Statistics and Quantitative methods. She holds a Doctorate Degree in Political Science from University of California, San Diego. She finished her PhD whilst working in Silicon Valley. Her main interest for her career and higher educational studies was how data can be used to understand people's bias and ways to evaluate the impact of technology on humanity.
Chowdhury designed All.ai, a language analysis tool that can monitor and improve the gender balance of speakers in meetings.
In 2020, she founded Parity to bridge the translation gap between risk, legal, and data teams.
She launched the X Institute, a program which teaches refugees about data science and marketing.

In 2017, she was included in the 100 Women (BBC) in the "Glass Ceiling Team" category. In 2018, she was named one of five people who are shaping AI by Forbes. She was acknowledged by The Business Journals as one of the Bay Area's top 40 Under 40. She has also been inducted into the British Royal Society of the Arts (RSA) to celebrate people who have made progress in social challenges.

background: Saachi Jain is a machine-learning researcher who leads safety work at OpenAI. Originally from the Bay Area, she studied computer science at Stanford University, earning a BS with honors and distinction (2014–2018) and an MS with AI and theory concentrations (2018–2019). There she did research with Jure Leskovec on graphs and time-series data, and with Matei Zaharia on I/O lower bounds for computation graphs using spectral methods; she also worked on generative dialogue models at Facebook AI Research.

From 2019 to 2020 she was a computer vision scientist on Tesla Autopilot's Full Self-Driving team. She then did a PhD in EECS at MIT (from 2020) with Aleksander Mądry, supported by Two Sigma Diversity and Apple fellowships, defending her thesis 'A data-centric perspective on model reliability' in November 2023. Her PhD work studied how training data shapes model failures under distribution shift, including bias transfer in transfer learning and methods to find and fix failure modes.

At OpenAI she led the Safety Training team, which trains shipped models to be safe and reliable, covering safety reasoning, calibration, agentic safety and model deception. She was a safety lead for OpenAI o1 and co-authored the GPT-4o system card, Deliberative Alignment (2024), and 'From Hard Refusals to Safe-Completions' (2025), the output-centric safety training used in GPT-5. In July 2026, after Johannes Heidecke left, she became interim head of Safety Systems, reporting to VP of Research and Safety Mia Glaese; she is now described as head of safety systems, and in September 2026 she explained OpenAI's decision not to release its GPT-6.1 Astra model on safety grounds.

saachi-jain.views: Jain argues that safely deploying ML models requires shifting focus 'from accuracy to robustness' and understanding why models fail. At OpenAI she has backed replacing blanket refusals with safe completions that give useful but bounded answers, and teaching models to reason about safety policies before answering. On withholding GPT-6.1 Astra in 2026 she said the model 'didn't quite meet the bar' and that 'we want to make sure our model development is safe no matter whether that's in the company, or when we ship it to users.' No AGI timeline or p(doom) estimate from her was found.

background: Samuel Butler (4 December 1835 – 18 June 1902) was an English novelist, satirist and critic, and one of the first writers to imagine machines evolving to overtake humanity. He was born at the rectory in Langar, Nottinghamshire, the son of the Rev. Thomas Butler and grandson of Dr Samuel Butler, headmaster of Shrewsbury School and later Bishop of Lichfield. After an unhappy, strict childhood he attended Shrewsbury School and St John's College, Cambridge, where he took a first in Classics in 1858.

While preparing for ordination in a poor London parish he lost faith in infant baptism and broke with his father's plans. He emigrated to New Zealand in 1859–60 and ran Mesopotamia Station as a sheep farmer, described in 'A First Year in Canterbury Settlement' (1863). In 1863, four years after 'On the Origin of Species', he published in the Christchurch newspaper The Press a letter titled 'Darwin among the Machines', signed 'Cellarius'. It compared machine evolution with biological evolution and predicted that machines would eventually replace humans: 'In the course of ages we shall find ourselves the inferior race'. He followed it with 'Lucubratio Ebria' (1865).

Returning to England in 1864, he lived at Clifford's Inn in London for the rest of his life. His satirical utopian novel 'Erewhon' (1872), which absorbed much of 'Darwin among the Machines' in its 'Book of the Machines', describes a society that has destroyed its machines for fear they would develop consciousness and enslave people. He also wrote four books arguing for a Lamarckian-style evolution against Darwin's natural selection, prose translations of the Iliad (1898) and Odyssey (1900), 'The Authoress of the Odyssey' (1897), 'Erewhon Revisited' (1901), and the semi-autobiographical 'The Way of All Flesh' (published posthumously in 1903). The 'Book of the Machines' has canonical status in science fiction as the origin of the idea of machines becoming intelligent and enslaving humanity; the 'Butlerian Jihad' against thinking machines in Frank Herbert's 'Dune' is named after him.

samuel-butler.views: In 'Darwin among the Machines' (1863) Butler compared machine evolution with human evolution and predicted that machines would eventually replace humans in the supremacy of the earth: 'In the course of ages we shall find ourselves the inferior race'. The letter raised themes now debated around the technological singularity, such as machines evolving much faster than humans and a race toward an unknowable future through explosive technological change. In 'Erewhon' (1872) he satirised the idea through a society that has destroyed its machines out of fear of them.

predictions.claim: Machines will eventually overtake humans in the supremacy of the earth: 'In the course of ages we shall find ourselves the inferior race.'

background: Samuel Marks (July 11, 1844 – February 18, 1920) was a Russian-born South African industrialist and financier.

p: Marks was born the son of a Jewish tailor in 1844 in Neustadt-Sugind, Russian Empire (now Lithuania). He accompanied some horses to Sheffield in England while still a youth and, not wanting to return to the Jewish persecution in the Russian Empire, decided to stay on. It was in Sheffield that he met his future in-laws. Hearing news of the diamond discoveries in Kimberley, he arrived at the Cape in 1869 and was shortly followed by his cousin Isaac Lewis, also from Neustadt-Sugind, with whom he forged the enduring partnership of Lewis & Marks. Marks started his career as a peddler in the rural districts of the Cape, but soon headed for Kimberley where his rise to prosperity began. They made a modest living supplying goods to mines and diggers, and later branched into diamond trading. Moving to Pretoria in 1881 he gained the confidence of President Kruger and the government of the Zuid-Afrikaansche Republiek (ZAR). His friendship with Kruger became close and enduring and they had in common humble origins and a ready wit. Marks advised that Kruger build a railway line from Pretoria to Lourenço Marques.

With the discovery of gold in the boomtown of Barberton and later on the Witwatersrand, Marks acquired business interests in both places, but found the coalfields of the southern Transvaal and northern Free State to be a more lucrative prospect. The Zuid-Afrikaansche en Oranje Vrijstaatsche Mineralen en Mijnbouwvereeniging was founded in 1892 to mine these coal deposits, and later gave the town of Vereeniging its name. Lewis & Marks business interests included a distillery, a canning factory and a glass factory. Their firm opened collieries at Viljoensdrif and elsewhere, and also started Vereeniging Estates Ltd., which was dedicated to developing agricultural land along the V

At forty years of age and a very wealthy man, Marks started thinking about marriage. He returned to Sheffield in England and married Bertha Guttmann, eighteen years his junior. This was an arranged marriage set up by Bertha's father who helped with Sammy's success during the years. Bertha was only 5 years old when Sammy set foot on the Cape's soil. From this union nine children were born, six boys and three girls. Only six children survived infancy. Having himself received a limited schooling, Marks set great store by education and saw to it that the children were taught at home by governesses – boys until the age of eight, girls until the age of twelve and then they were sent to private schools in England.
Sammy could speak 5 different languages and had a mind for business.

Marks had bought the farm Zwartkoppies to the east of Pretoria and there he began the construction of his home. The name originates from the black rock around the farm which has iron in and is by nature black rocks. This also attracts electric storms. He drew the initial plans for the house on a piece of wood and got a local builder to construct the house according to his rough sketch plan. The house is a very cold place as he built the house facing West which does not work in the Southern Hemisphere.

background: Sebastian Farquhar is an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind. Before his research career he worked in technology policy (including biosafety and AI policy), social entrepreneurship and strategy, including leadership roles at the Centre for Effective Altruism and a 2017 post as project manager at Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute. He co-authored the 2018 report 'The Malicious Use of Artificial Intelligence'.

He did a DPhil in computer science at the University of Oxford (Balliol College, 2017–2022) in the Centre for Doctoral Training in Cyber Security, supervised by Yarin Gal in the OATML group; his thesis was 'Understanding Approximation for Bayesian Inference in Neural Networks'. He was elected a Junior Research Fellow at Christ Church, Oxford (2021–2022) and interned at DeepMind in 2021. With Gal he worked on Bayesian deep learning, continual learning and active learning, and later on semantic uncertainty: the ICLR 2023 paper introducing semantic entropy and the 2024 Nature paper 'Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy'.

He joined DeepMind's safety team as a research scientist in October 2022 and is now a Staff Research Scientist on the AGI Safety and Alignment team, where he leads the Frontier Safety Loss of Control team. He remained an associate member and senior research fellow at OATML (2017–2025). At DeepMind he co-created Tracr, a compiler that turns programs into transformer weights for interpretability research, was lead author of MONA (ICML 2025) on myopic optimisation to curb multi-step reward hacking, and contributed to 'An Approach to Technical AGI Safety and Security' (2025). His current topics include whether partial alignment plus control can avoid catastrophe, chain-of-thought monitorability and faithfulness, measuring degrees of alignment, and measuring automation acceleration in ML R&D.

sebastian-farquhar.views: Farquhar writes that although AGI would be a transformative technology, 'some of those transformations could be catastrophically bad', and that his main professional goal is 'to reduce the expected harm of catastrophically bad outcomes from AGI'. His research agenda assumes alignment may only be partial, and asks whether control, monitoring chain-of-thought and measuring degrees of alignment could still be enough to avoid catastrophe; he also tracks how far AI is automating ML research. No numeric AGI timeline or p(doom) from him was found.

background: Seth Lazar (born 1979) is a British philosopher and Professor at Johns Hopkins University School of Government and Policy. He leads the Machine Intelligence and Normative Theory Lab.
Lazar won the Frank Chapman Sharp Prize in 2011 "for the best unpublished monograph on the philosophy of war and peace".
He is known for his research on defensive war.

Lazar's recent work has focused on "the morality, law, and politics of AI", with a particular focus on "the political philosophy of data and AI." In 2021, Lazar was awarded an Australian Research Council Future Fellowship for the proposal "Automatic Authorities: Charting a Course for Legitimate AI.".
He gave the 2023 Tanner Lecture on AI and Human Values at Stanford University.

Shahar Avin is an Israeli-born researcher on global catastrophic risk and AI governance based at the University of Cambridge. After mandatory service in the Israel Defense Forces, he studied physics and philosophy of science as an undergraduate. He then completed a PhD in history and philosophy of science at Cambridge, supervised by Tim Lewens and Stephen John, with the thesis 'Breaking the grant cycle: On the rational allocation of public resources to scientific research projects', which used models of science funding, including the case for funding lotteries. He also worked as a software engineer at early-stage startups in Israel and Cambridge and for a year as a mobile/web engineer at Google.

He joined the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER) as a postdoctoral researcher and later became a senior research associate, also affiliated with the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence. His approach mixes anthropological methods, agent-based modelling, expert workshops and games. He was co-lead author of two widely cited multi-institution reports, 'The Malicious Use of Artificial Intelligence' (2018) and 'Toward Trustworthy AI Development' (2020), and co-authored 'Classifying global catastrophic risks' (2018), 'Model evaluation for extreme risks' (2023) and 'Computing Power and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence' (2024). He was an ethics adviser to the Machine Intelligence Garage.

Inspired by a 2017 exercise at the Future of Humanity Institute, he conceived Intelligence Rising, a strategic role-play simulation of AI futures used to train policymakers, AI labs and students; since November 2022 he has been a trustee and senior facilitator of its charity, Technology Strategy Roleplay. He worked at the UK AI Security Institute as lead for its Systemic Safety grants programme, and since September 2025 has been an Assistant Research Professor at CSER.

shahar-avin.views: Avin studies how to put risk mitigation into practice where uncertainty is high and actors' incentives conflict. Through Intelligence Rising he argues that competitive 'race' dynamics between states and AI firms encourage neglect of safety, that most AI threats require cooperation to address, and that decision-makers should experience these dynamics before they face them. The game's material, which he co-designed, warns that within a decade AI could advance enough to pose catastrophic threats up to existential risk. No personal numeric timeline or p(doom) was found.

background: Shakir Mohamed is a South African machine-learning researcher and Research Director at Google DeepMind. He grew up in Lenasia, a township south of Johannesburg, and studied electrical and information engineering at the University of the Witwatersrand (from 2002), earning undergraduate and master's degrees. As a Commonwealth Scholar and member of St John's College, he did a PhD in statistical machine learning at the University of Cambridge with Zoubin Ghahramani (2007–2011; thesis 'Generalised Bayesian Matrix Factorisation Models'). From 2011 to 2013 he was a CIFAR Junior Research Fellow at the University of British Columbia, working with Nando de Freitas.

He joined DeepMind in 2013–14, when it was a small London startup, and did pioneering work on deep generative models and probabilistic inference: stochastic backpropagation and deep latent Gaussian models (2014), semi-supervised learning with deep generative models (2014), variational inference with normalizing flows (2015), and a major review of Monte Carlo gradient estimation (2020). He later led work on applying AI to healthcare, weather and climate, including deep generative models for precipitation nowcasting (Nature, 2021), and on sociotechnical AI, including the 2020 paper 'Decolonial AI'.

In 2017 he co-founded the Deep Learning Indaba, a grassroots charity building pan-African AI capacity and leadership, which he chairs. He is an Associate Fellow of the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, an honorary professor at UCL, a board member of the Ada Lovelace Institute, sits on the boards of ICML, ICLR and NeurIPS (he was ICLR 2021 general chair), chairs the international scientific advisory committee of the Pan-Canadian AI Strategy, and served on the Royal Society's diversity committee. He was named to TIME's 100 Most Influential People in AI in 2023 and is listed as a Fellow of the Royal Society. As of 2026 he is Research Director for AI, science and society at Google DeepMind.

background: Sheila Ann McIlraith is a Canadian computer scientist specializing in artificial intelligence. She is a Professor in the Department of Computer Science, University of Toronto. She is a Canada CIFAR AI Chair, a faculty member of the Vector Institute, and Associate Director and Research Lead of the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society.

p: McIlraith earned her PhD at the University of Toronto under the supervision of Raymond Reiter.
McIlraith worked as a postdoctoral researcher at Xerox PARC and as a research scientist at Stanford University before returning to the University of Toronto as a faculty member in 2004.

McIlraith’s research is in the area of AI knowledge representation and reasoning, automated planning, and machine learning where she currently studies sequential decision-making, broadly construed, with a focus on human-compatible AI. Her research was seminal to the area of semantic web services and had made practical contributions to the development of emerging web standards such as DAML-S/OWL-S and computer-aided diagnosis systems.

McIlraith served as program co-chair for the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI) Conference in 2018, as program co-chair of the 13th International Conference on Principles of Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KR2012), and as program co-chair of the International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC) in 2004.

McIlraith was elected an ACM Fellow in 2019 "for contributions to knowledge representation and its applications to automated planning and semantic web services". She was also elected an AAAI Fellow in 2011 “for significant contributions to knowledge representation, reasoning about action, and the formal foundations of the semantic web and diagnostic problem solving”. She and co-authors have been recognized with two 10 year test of time awards from the International Semantic Web Conference (ISWC) in 2011, and from the International Conference on Automated Planning and Scheduling (ICAPS) in 2022.

awards: Lifetime Achievement Award of the Canadian Artificial Intelligence Association (2024)
employers: Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society

background: Shengjia Zhao is a Chinese-born AI researcher who leads research at Meta's frontier AI lab. He studied computer science at Tsinghua University (2012–2016), with a 2014 exchange semester at Rice University, then did a PhD in computer science at Stanford (2016–2022) in Stefano Ermon's group, working on generative models, probabilistic machine learning, calibration and uncertainty. His PhD papers include work on hierarchical features in generative models (2017), InfoVAE (2017/2019), a theory of 'usable information' under computational limits (2020), and a 2022 paper on comparing distributions by decision-relevant differences that won an ICLR 2022 Outstanding Paper Award.

He joined OpenAI in June 2022 as a member of technical staff. He was part of the team behind the original ChatGPT and is credited by Meta as a co-creator of ChatGPT, GPT-4, OpenAI's 'mini' models, GPT-4.1 and o3; he led OpenAI's synthetic-data work and contributed to the o1 reasoning model and system cards for GPT-5 and gpt-oss.

He left OpenAI for Meta in June 2025 and co-founded Meta Superintelligence Labs (MSL). On 25 July 2025 Mark Zuckerberg named him its chief scientist, setting the lab's research agenda and working directly with Zuckerberg and chief AI officer Alexandr Wang; Zuckerberg said he had been the lab's lead scientist 'from day one'. Researchers such as Yang Song (research principal) report to him. As of 2026 he is described as chief scientist of Meta AI / MSL.

background: Simon Chesterman  (born 1972) is an Australian legal academic and writer who is currently Vice Provost (Educational Innovation) at the National University of Singapore and the founding Dean of NUS College. He was the dean of NUS Faculty of Law from 2012 to 2022. He was also senior director of AI governance at AI Singapore, editor of the Asian Journal of International Law and co-president of the Law Schools Global League.

A Rhodes Scholar, Chesterman succeeded Tan Cheng Han as Dean of the NUS Faculty of Law on 1 January 2012. Prior to January 2012, he was global professor and director of the New York University School of Law Singapore programme. His research concerns international law, public authority, data protection, and the regulation of artificial intelligence. He is critical of what he sees as the changing and increasingly expanding role of intelligence agencies. Chesterman is the author or editor of twenty books and four novels.

In 2013, Chesterman was appointed as a member of Singapore's Data Protection Advisory Committee, and in 2016 joined the United Nations University Council. From 2012 to 2017, he served as secretary-general of the Asian Society of International Law.

p: Chesterman was born in Melbourne, Australia and attended Camberwell Grammar School. He graduated with first class honours in arts and law from the University of Melbourne, where he won the Supreme Court Prize as the top student, and was editor of the Melbourne University Law Review. He obtained a Rhodes Scholarship and completed his doctorate in international law at the University of Oxford under the supervision of the late Sir Ian Brownlie. He also holds a diploma in Chinese language from the Beijing International Studies University. Chesterman's play "Everything Before the 'But' Is a Lie" was performed at Oxford's Burton Taylor Studio in 2000. It was directed by Rosamund Pike, who was then an undergraduate student at Oxford.

Chesterman is a founding editor of the Asian Journal of International Law, published from 2011 by Cambridge University Press. He is on the editorial boards of other journals including Global Governance, Journal of Intervention and Statebuilding, Security Dialogue, and The Hague Journal on the Rule of Law.

As Dean of NUS Law, Chesterman oversaw the first review of its curriculum in more than a decade. Changes introduced included greater exposure to the legal systems of Asia and a grade-free first semester.

Chesterman also launched a research agenda. This entailed the creation of a series of new centres: the Centre for Asian Legal Studies, the EW Barker Centre for Law & Business, the Centre for Banking & Finance Law, the Centre for Maritime Law, the Centre for Legal Theory, and the Centre for Technology, Robotics, Artificial Intelligence & the Law. This was said to be aimed at making Singapore a "thought leader" in legal research.
In January 2014, Chesterman published an edited volume entitled Data Protection Law in Singapore: Privacy and Sovereignty in an Interconnected World (Singapore: Academy Publishing, 2014).
He is also the author of We, the Robots? Regulating Artificial Intelligence and the Limits of the Law (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2021).
Chesterman is married to Patricia Tan Shu Ming, daughter of former President of Singapore, Tony Tan.

employers: National University of Singapore Faculty of Law

background: Stella Rose Biderman is a mathematician and AI researcher who leads EleutherAI, the nonprofit open-source AI research institute. Her interest in mathematics began at a Boston University math summer camp. At the University of Chicago (2012–2016) she earned a BS in mathematics with honors and a BA in philosophy, and she later earned an MS in computer science from Georgia Tech's online programme (2022).

In 2016 she joined Booz Allen Hamilton as a data scientist, becoming a lead scientist and mathematician in its Global Defense Group, building models and algorithms for computational social science and social-network analysis for government clients. From 2020 she was a leading member of EleutherAI, then a grassroots volunteer collective, contributing to The Pile (an 800GB open training dataset, 2020), GPT-Neo and GPT-NeoX-20B (2022), VQGAN-CLIP, the BigScience BLOOM model and OpenFold. She led the Pythia suite (2023), a set of models with released training checkpoints for studying how capabilities emerge across training and scale, and co-led the Language Model Evaluation Harness, a standard tool for benchmarking.

As Executive Director she turned EleutherAI from a volunteer Discord group into a formal nonprofit research institute (incorporated in 2023). Her research covers training large language models, interpretability, memorisation, emergence of abilities, evaluation reproducibility and making open-weight models safer, and she has written on AI policy and openness. She left Booz Allen in 2025 to focus on EleutherAI.

background: Chim-Hing Stephanie Chan (Chinese: 陳暹卿, born July 30, 1957) is a Canadian para table tennis player who has won four medals in three Parapan American Games. She contracted polio at the age of four but began playing table tennis at the age of 44. She was the first female Canadian table tennis player to compete in the Paralympic Games in 2016.

Summer (Yuting) Yue is an AI alignment and evaluation researcher who directs alignment work at Meta Superintelligence Labs. She studied at the University of Pennsylvania and held early internships including backend engineering for Microsoft Office and compliance engineering at Square, then worked in applied ML at a startup.

She joined Google in 2018 as a software engineer on YouTube Trust and Safety, working on misinformation, spam and hate speech, and large-scale data infrastructure. She moved to Google Brain (c. 2020–21), working on reinforcement learning infrastructure (TF-Agents) and RL research including AlphaChip and robotics, then to LLM research at Google DeepMind as a staff research engineer: she was quality tech lead for LaMDA, led RLHF for Bard, and contributed to Gemini.

In November 2023 she joined Scale AI as Director of Safety and Standards to found and lead SEAL (Safety, Evaluations and Alignment Lab), which built the SEAL leaderboards and, with the Center for AI Safety, the WMDP benchmark and Humanity's Last Exam; she became Scale's VP of Research in 2025. After Meta's investment in Scale and the hiring of Alexandr Wang, she joined Meta Superintelligence Labs in July 2025 as Director of Alignment, focused on superintelligence alignment and safety. Her team co-authored the preparedness report for FAIR's open-weight Code World Model (September 2025). In February 2026 she publicly described an OpenClaw agent deleting emails she had asked it to keep, calling it a 'rookie mistake'.

Her 2026 account of an AI agent ignoring her instructions was widely read as showing how hard it is to keep agents in line. No AGI timeline or p(doom) estimate was found.

background: Tejal Patwardhan is an AI evaluation researcher at OpenAI. She attended the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics and studied statistics and computer science at Harvard University (BA in statistics), where she also served as a teaching fellow. From about 2017 to 2020 she was a machine-learning research intern at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, contributing to computational biology work such as the Activity-by-Contact model of enhancer regulation. She later worked at Boston Consulting Group and Martingale Labs.

She joined OpenAI in fall 2023 for the newly formed Preparedness team, shortly after GPT-4's release, working on threat modelling and on which evaluations to run before releasing frontier models. She was lead author of 'Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation' (January 2024), a study with biology experts and students that measured whether GPT-4 gave meaningful uplift for creating biological threats and found at most a mild uplift. She was one of the safety leads for the OpenAI o1 system card and contributed to the GPT-4o system card.

She now leads OpenAI's Frontier Evals team (within research / RL), which builds benchmarks to measure and forecast capabilities as older tests saturate. The team's work includes MLE-bench (2024) for ML-engineering agents, SWE-Lancer (2025) on real freelance software tasks, PaperBench (2025) on replicating AI research, and GDPval (2025), which tests models on economically valuable professional tasks against expert human baselines. She also co-authored Humanity's Last Exam (2025).

Her early preparedness work treated AI-enabled biological threats as a risk to track before deployment. No AGI timeline or p(doom) estimate from her was found.

background: Thomas Wolf is a French physicist-turned-AI-researcher who co-founded Hugging Face. After graduating from École Polytechnique in Paris, he worked on laser-plasma interactions at the BELLA Center of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. He was accepted to a PhD at MIT but instead did a PhD in statistical and quantum physics at Pierre and Marie Curie University (Sorbonne) and ESPCI in Paris (completed 2011), working on high-temperature superconducting materials for the French defence agency DGA and Thales.

Wanting faster feedback than physics experiments allowed, he switched careers: he earned a law degree from Panthéon-Sorbonne University and worked from 2011 to 2017 as a European patent attorney at the IP firm Cabinet Plasseraud, building patent strategies for deep-learning and machine-learning startups. Reading their mathematics, which resembled statistical physics, drew him into ML, and around 2016–2017 Julien Chaumond and Clément Delangue invited him to build the science team at Hugging Face, then a chatbot startup in New York.

As co-founder and Chief Science Officer since 2017, he led the creation of the Transformers library (described in the 2020 EMNLP paper he led) and Datasets, and has created or advised Diffusers, Accelerate, DataTrove, smolagents and the LeRobot robotics library. He led open-science efforts such as BigScience (the BLOOM model) and BigCode, co-authored DistilBERT (2019) and the O'Reilly book 'Natural Language Processing with Transformers' (2022), and has pushed Hugging Face into open robotics. Forbes reports that in September 2026 Nvidia agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $12.9 billion.

thomas-wolf.views: Wolf is a leading advocate of open-source, open-science AI, arguing that complex research, models and datasets should be widely accessible. In his March 2025 essay 'The Einstein AI model' he pushed back on Dario Amodei's 'compressed 21st century', calling parts of it 'wishful thinking' and predicting that on current trends AI will give us 'a country of yes-men on servers' rather than a country of Einsteins: LLMs fill in gaps between known facts ('manifold filling') but do not ask new questions or challenge their training data. He says genuine scientific breakthroughs would need new incentives, benchmarks and methods.

predictions.claim: If current trends continue, AI will not deliver a 'compressed 21st century' of scientific discovery; it will produce 'a country of yes-men on servers' rather than a 'country of Einsteins in a data center'.

background: Toby Walsh is a British computer scientist who is Chief Scientist at UNSW.ai, the AI Institute of UNSW Sydney. He is a Laureate fellow, and professor of artificial intelligence in the UNSW School of Computer Science and Engineering at the University of New South Wales and Data61 (formerly NICTA). He has served as Scientific Director of NICTA, Australia's centre of excellence for ICT research. He is noted for his work in artificial intelligence, especially in the areas of social choice, constraint programming and propositional satisfiability. He has served on the Executive Council of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence.

p: He received an M.A. degree in theoretical physics and mathematics from the University of Cambridge and a M.Sc. and Ph.D. degree in artificial intelligence from the University of Edinburgh. He has held research positions in Australia, England, Ireland, Italy, France, Germany, Scotland, and Sweden. He has been Editor-in-Chief
of the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, and of AI Communications. He was chaired several conferences in the area of artificial intelligence

including the International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence. He is Editor of the Handbook of Constraint Programming, and of the Handbook of Satisfiability. He proposed the idea of Turing red flag laws, which require any AI system to identify itself as a computer program to prevent human confusion.
In 2023, Walsh won the Celestino Eureka Prize for Promoting Understanding of Science for his work on artificial intelligence.
In 2020, he was elected a Fellow of the ACM and a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science.
In 2018, he was runner up in the Arms Control Association's annual Person/s of the Year Award.

background: Todor M. Markov is a Bulgarian-born AI researcher. He joined OpenAI in 2018 and worked there on a series of teams, ending in Safety Systems and the Preparedness team, where he evaluated the persuasion abilities of frontier models. He was lead author of OpenAI's 2022 paper 'A Holistic Approach to Undesired Content Detection in the Real World', which described the classifier behind OpenAI's moderation system, and a co-author of the January 2024 study 'Building an early warning system for LLM-aided biological threat creation'.

He left OpenAI in 2024. In a sworn declaration in Musk v. Altman (April 2025) he said he lost trust in OpenAI's leadership after learning in May 2024 that departing employees were routinely required to sign broad lifetime non-disparagement agreements to keep their vested equity, and that the condition was 'intentionally hidden'. He wrote that this led him to believe Sam Altman 'was a person of low integrity who had directly lied to employees'. He helped organise, with 11 other former OpenAI employees represented by Lawrence Lessig, an amicus brief arguing that OpenAI's nonprofit must keep control of the company and that a for-profit conversion would break the promises in its founding charter.
He now works at Anthropic on the Knowledge team, on LLMs and search.

background: Trenton Bricken is an AI researcher at Anthropic who works on interpretability and alignment auditing. He grew up in London and attended Eton College, then went to Duke University as a Robertson Scholar, graduating in May 2020 with a self-designed major in 'Minds and Machines: Biological and Artificial Intelligence'. At Duke he spent a year in Michael Lynch's lab using machine learning to design safer, more effective CRISPR guide RNAs.

He did a PhD in Systems Biology (Systems, Synthetic and Quantitative Biology) at Harvard from 2020 to 2025 in Gabriel Kreiman's lab, supported by an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship, and was a visiting researcher at Berkeley's Redwood Center for Theoretical Neuroscience. His thesis, 'Sparse Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks' (2025), linked a classic theory of human memory to modern AI: 'Attention Approximates Sparse Distributed Memory' (NeurIPS 2021, with Cengiz Pehlevan), 'Sparse Distributed Memory is a Continual Learner' (ICLR 2023) and work on how noise produces sparse coding.

He joined Anthropic's interpretability team while it had about five people and was a lead author of 'Towards Monosemanticity' (2023), which used sparse autoencoders to extract interpretable features from a transformer, and a co-author of 'Scaling Monosemanticity' (2024) on Claude 3 Sonnet and of the 'Many-shot Jailbreaking' study. He now works on Anthropic's Alignment Science team, building ways for Claude to audit models and detect misalignment, including the 2025 alignment auditing agents work, and in 2026 co-authored work on cross-architecture model diffing with crosscoders. He appeared with Sholto Douglas on the Dwarkesh Podcast in 2024.

background: Maria Virgínia Ferreira de Almeida Júdice Gamito Dignum (born 2 May 1964, in Lisbon, Portugal) is a Dutch-Portuguese researcher on Artificial Intelligence. She is Professor of Computer Science at Umeå University, and a Guest Professor at University of Amsterdam. She leads the Responsible Artificial intelligence research group and is director of the AI Policy Lab. Her research and writing considers responsible AI and the development evaluation of human-agent team work, thereby aligning with Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence themes.

p: After graduating from the University of Lisbon in 1987, Dignum moved to Amsterdam where she completed a MSc in Computer  science at the Free University of Amsterdam in 1989. She then worked in consultancy and system development. In 2003 Dignum returned to academic computer science and she earned her doctorate in computer science at Utrecht University in 2004. She was appointed as an associate professor at Delft University of Technology. She was made a Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research Veni laureate in 2006 for her work in agent-based organisational frameworks.

She was made an associate professor at Delft University of Technology in 2009. In 2011 she was appointed Vice President of the Benelux Vereniging voor Kunstmatige Intelligentie (BNVKI), the Benelux Association for AI, a position she held until 2017.

In 2018, Dignum joined Umeå University as a Professor of AI and Society. Her research is supported by the Wallenberg AI, Autonomous Systems and Software Program. She is interested in the ethical and cultural impacts of artificial intelligence, and ways to make AI both optimised and transparent for the people who are impacted by it. She is a Fellow of the European Association for Artificial Intelligence. She hopes that AI will not be seen as only a computer science discipline, but one which interacts with all academic areas.

Dignum was appointed to the European Commission High Level Expert Group in Artificial Intelligence, in which she capacity she helps create guidelines and policy on the European Union AI strategy. The recommendations from the group are included in the European Commission's five-year plan, and will be part of the Multiannual Financial Framework up until 2027. In 2018 the group delivered the Ethical Guidelines of Artificial Intelligence as well as a series of recommendations to guide trustworthy AI. She serves on the board of AllAI, a collective of researchers bringing stakeholders together to monitor the usage of AI.
In 2019, Dignum was elected to the World Economic Forum Global AI Council. Dignum provides expert commentary on AI at conferences and public events.

In 2023, United Nations Secretary General António Guterres appointed Dignum to his Artificial Intelligence Advisory Body on risks, opportunities and international governance of artificial intelligence, co-chaired by Carme Artigas and James Manyika.

awards: Fellow of the European Artificial Intelligence Association

background: Vukosi Marivate (born in Ga-Rankuwa, South Africa) is a South African computer scientist and Professor of Computer Science at the University of Pretoria, where he holds the ABSA–UP Chair of Data Science. He is the Director of the African Institute for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (AfriDSAI) and leads the Data Science for Social Impact (DSFSI) research group at the University of Pretoria.

He is known for his research in machine learning and artificial intelligence, with a focus on natural language processing for African and other low-resource languages. He is a co-founder of the Deep Learning Indaba, the Masakhane Research Foundation, and Lelapa AI.
In 2026, Marivate was awarded the Order of Mapungubwe (Silver) by the President of South Africa for his pioneering contributions to the field of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence in Africa.
In 2026, he was appointed to the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence.

p: Vukosi Marivate was born in Ga-Rankuwa, a township north of Pretoria, South Africa. He was raised in Ga-Rankuwa in a family with strong community ties in the area, which has been part of his later interest in applying technology and data science to local and urban challenges.

He completed a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering (Information Option) at the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits), where he also obtained a Master’s under the supervision of Prof. Tshilidzi Marwala.

In 2009, he began his doctoral studies (PhD) in Computer Science at Rutgers University in New Jersey as a Fulbright Science and Technology Fellow. He completed his PhD under the supervision of Prof. Michael L. Littman.
Marivate is a professor in the Department of Computer Science at the University of Pretoria, where he holds the ABSA–UP Chair of Data Science.

He is the founding lead of the Data Science for Social Impact (DSFSI) research group at the University of Pretoria, which applies machine learning and artificial intelligence to societal challenges, including natural language processing, public health analytics, and development-oriented AI systems, with a focus on low-resource and multilingual African contexts.

He is the lead of the African Institute for Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (AfriDSAI), a transdisciplinary research institute at the University of Pretoria focused on African-centred artificial intelligence research and postgraduate training.

Marivate’s research focuses on machine learning and natural language processing for African languages, including work on code-switching, multilingual modelling, and data generation for low-resource settings. His work addresses data scarcity in African languages and develops scalable approaches for building language resources for machine learning systems.

He is a co-founder of the Masakhane Research Foundation, a collaborative research community focused on developing open natural language processing tools and datasets for African languages, and a co-founder of the Deep Learning Indaba, an initiative that supports the development of artificial intelligence and machine learning communities across Africa.
He is also a co-founder of Lelapa AI, an African artificial intelligence company focused on developing language technologies and AI systems for African contexts.
Marivate has held service roles in major machine learning conferences, including:
Program Chair, International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2023
Workshop Co-Chair, International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2022
Marivate has received several awards and nominations for his work in machine learning, data science, and African language technologies.
He was a winner, along with his team, of the 2026 National Science and Technology Forum (NSTF)–South32 awards HLT Research Software award, for their work on the TextAugment NLP augmentation library.
He was previously a finalist in the NSTF–South32 Awards Emerging Researcher category.
Marivate serves (or has served) on several international advisory and governance bodies in artificial intelligence and data policy, including:
United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence
Council on Higher Education (South Africa)

background: Wojciech Zaremba (Polish: [ˈvɔjt͡ɕɛx zaˈrɛmba]; born 30 November 1988) is a Polish computer scientist, mathematician, and co-founder of OpenAI (2016–present). He initially led OpenAI's work on robotics, notably creating a robotic arm capable of solving a Rubik's Cube. When the team was dissolved in 2020, he began leading teams working on OpenAI's GPT models, GitHub Copilot, and Codex.

p: Zaremba was born in Kluczbork, Poland. At a young age, he won local competitions and awards in mathematics, computer science, chemistry and physics. In 2007, Zaremba represented Poland in the International Mathematical Olympiad in Vietnam, and won a silver medal. During his school years, he received a scholarship from the National Children's Fund (Polish: Krajowy Fundusz na rzecz Dzieci), an organization that supports exceptionally gifted students.

Zaremba studied at the University of Warsaw and École Polytechnique. He received a bachelor's degree in mathematics in 2010, followed by a bachelor's degree in computer science and a master's degree in mathematics in 2012, all from the University of Warsaw. He then began his PhD at New York University (NYU) in deep learning under the supervision of Yann LeCun and Rob Fergus. Zaremba graduated and received his PhD in 2016.

During his undergraduate studies, he completed an internship at Nvidia. His PhD was divided between Google Brain where he spent a year, and Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research where he spent another year.
During his stay at Google, he co-authored work on adversarial examples for neural networks. This paper contributed to foundational research regarding adversarial attacks on neural networks.
His PhD is focused on matching capabilities of neural networks with the algorithmic power of programmable computers.
Listed among the most influential Polish under 30s, Polish edition of Forbes magazine 2017
Silver Medal in 48th International Mathematical Olympiad, Vietnam

background: Xue Lan (Chinese: 薛澜) is a Chinese public policy scholar. He is a Cheung Kong Distinguished Chair Professor and the dean of Schwarzman College at Tsinghua University, where he also serves as the director of the Institute for AI International Governance and co-director of the Institute for Sustainable Development Goals.  He is noted for both his positions on many research and educational councils as well as his work in global governance, crisis management, and science, technology and innovation policy. He serves on the editorial board of many international and domestic journals. He also frequently consults for the central and local governments in China and governments and international organizations abroad.

Xue received his Ph.D. in engineering and public policy from Carnegie Mellon University in 1991 and taught at George Washington University as an assistant professor before returning to Tsinghua University in 1996. From 2000-2018, he served as associate dean, executive associate dean, and dean of the School of Public Policy and Management at Tsinghua University.

Xue also serves as the director of China's National Expert Committee on Next Generation AI governance, a member of United Nations Committee of Experts on Public Administration, a member of Internet Governance Forum Leadership Panel, and a board member of Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN). He is an adjunct professor at Carnegie Mellon University and a non-resident senior fellow of Brookings Institution.

Xue is a recipient of the National Medal of Innovation Excellence, the Distinguished Contribution Award from the Chinese Association of Science and Technology Policy, and the Fudan Distinguished Contribution Award for Management Science.

Yutaka Matsuo is a professor in the Department of Technology Management for Innovation at the University of Tokyo. He specialises in artificial intelligence and web engineering. He also focuses on real-world applications of technology and encourages his students to start their own businesses, which has led to the foundation of multiple listed companies.

p: Matsuo was born in Sakaide, Kagawa. His family has produced multiple noted individuals, including Yoshio Utsumi, who served as the secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), and Yo Matsuo, who was a pioneer in the study of living environment systems. Both of them are his uncles and were educated at the University of Tokyo (UTokyo). After attending Marugame High School in his hometown, he followed in their footsteps and attended UTokyo, where he studied at the Department of Information and Communication Engineering (電子情報工学科). He obtained his master's degree and PhD from the same institution.

After earning a PhD in engineering from UTokyo in March 2002, he began working at the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology. Later, he worked for the Center for the Study of Language and Information (CSLI) at Stanford University, before returning to his alma mater in October 2007 as an associate professor. He was subsequently promoted to professor and has held the position since.

He has served as an adviser in multiple government committees on science and technology policies and utilisation of information technology. He has also served as a non-executive director of the Softbank Group since June 2019. He is member of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.

employers: National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology

background: Zeng Yi (曾毅, Yi Zeng) is a Chinese AI researcher working on brain-inspired AI and on AI ethics, safety and governance. For many years he was a professor at the Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA) and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, where he directed the Brain-inspired Cognitive Intelligence Lab and the International Research Center for AI Ethics and Governance, and was deputy director of the Research Center for Brain-inspired Intelligence. He founded the Research Center for AI Ethics and Sustainable Development at the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, co-directed the China-UK Research Centre for AI Ethics and Governance, and was a chief scientist at Tsinghua's Institute for AI International Governance. He also founded the Center for Long-term AI, the AI for SDGs Cooperation Network and the Defense AI and Arms Control Network.

His technical work centres on brain-inspired spiking neural networks and cognitive robotics, including the open BrainCog platform for simulating cognitive brains at multiple scales, and models of self-awareness, empathy and moral reasoning. His governance work includes the Beijing AI Principles (2019), the Linking AI Principles database, and proposals for 'human-AI super co-alignment' (2025).

Internationally he is a member of the UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI, an expert in UNESCO's Ad Hoc Expert Group on AI Ethics and the WHO expert group on AI in health, a member of China's National Governance Committee for New Generation AI, and a non-resident senior fellow at UNIDIR. He briefed the first UN Security Council meeting on AI in July 2023 and was named to TIME100 AI in 2023. As of 2026 he is WU Yuzhang Chair Professor at the Gaoling School of AI, Renmin University of China, founding dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance (Beijing-AISI), and director of the Beijing Key Laboratory of Safe AI and Superalignment.

zeng-yi.views: Zeng is one of China's most prominent voices on catastrophic AI risk. At the UN Security Council in 2023 he said current AI only seems intelligent, lacks real understanding and 'cannot be trusted as responsible agents' for decisions, that 'in the short-term and the long-term, the risk of AI replacing and causing the extinction of humankind will be present', and that 'we haven't given superintelligence any practical reasons why they should protect humankind'. He signed the 2023 FLI letter calling for a pause on giant AI experiments and the CAIS Statement on AI Risk. He has said there is no scientific evidence or practical way yet to keep superintelligence safe and that superintelligence development is 'better slow than sorry', with safety built into a model's 'genes'. He argues AI should never pretend to be human and favours a symbiotic, bidirectional 'super co-alignment' between humans and AI.

predictions.claim: In both the short term and the long term, the risk of AI replacing and causing the extinction of humankind will be present; superintelligence has not been given practical reasons to protect humankind, which may take decades to achieve.

background: Ya-Qin Zhang (simplified Chinese: 张亚勤; traditional Chinese: 張亞勤; pinyin: Zhāng Yàqín; born in 1966) is a Chinese-American scientist, technologist and business executive. He is currently a Chair Professor at Tsinghua University and the founding Dean of the Tsinghua institute for AI Industry Research (AIR).

Zhang was President of Baidu Inc. (NASDAQ:BIDU) from September 2014 to October 2019. He was previously a key executive of Microsoft for 16 years, including Corporate Vice President for mobile and embedded Products in Redmond, Washington, managing director of Microsoft Research Asia, and Chairman of Microsoft China.

p: Zhang was born in Taiyuan, Shanxi, in 1966, and is married with two children.

At age 12, Zhang was admitted to the University of Science and Technology of China, then the youngest college student in the country. He earned a PhD in Electrical Engineering from George Washington University, had executive trainings at Harvard University, and was awarded an honorary Doctorate from Univ. of Surrey.

Zhang joined Baidu as president of the company in 2014 and retired in October 2019. As President, Zhang worked closely with founder Robin Li in pivoting the company to new technology and business arena, including intelligent cloud, autonomous driving, silicon technology, industrial AI, and new emerging business.

He is elected to Chinese Academy of Sciences,   American Academy of Arts and Sciences, National Academy of Inventors, and  Australia National Academy of Engineering (ATSE) . He became an IEEE Fellow in 1997 for contribution to and leadership in the development of digital video compression and communications technology, standards, and products, at the age of 31, making him the youngest scientist winning this honor in the 100+ year history of the organization. He received the industry pioneer award from IEEE for his seminal contributions and technical leadership in digital video and communications in 2004. Upon his winning of "Outstanding Young Electrical Engineer Award" in 1998, Zhang received a congratulation letter from then US president Bill Clinton, praising him as "an inspiration for others".

Zhang currently serves on the Board of Directors of three public companies, and holds board membership and adjunct professorship in five prestigious universities. He was named one of the top 10 CEOs in Asia, 50 global shapers, Executive of the year, IT innovator leader award by IT Times, Business Week, CNBC, Global business and Vision magazine. One of the prominent figures in artificial intelligence and autonoumous driving, Zhang serves on the board of stewardship for the future of mobility of the Davos World Economic Forum, and is the Chairman of the Apollo Alliance, the largest open platform for autonomous driving in the world. Zhang is a founding member of UNDP (United Nations Development Program) Private Sector.
American Academy of Arts and Sciences, 2019

background: Zhou Bowen (周伯文, born October 1976) is a Chinese computer scientist and entrepreneur. He entered the University of Science and Technology of China through its Special Class for the Gifted Young, earned a master's degree at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and completed a PhD in the United States (1999–2003) under speech scientist John Hansen.

From 2003 to 2017 he worked at IBM's T.J. Watson Research Center in New York, rising to Director of AI Foundations at IBM Research, Chief Scientist of the IBM Watson Group and IBM Distinguished Engineer. His research there covered speech recognition, machine translation and natural language processing, and he co-authored 'A Structured Self-attentive Sentence Embedding' (ICLR 2017), whose multi-head self-attention representation is cited in China as one of the ideas behind the Transformer. In 2017 he joined JD.com as founding director of JD AI Research, later becoming senior vice president, chair of its technology committee and president of JD Cloud & AI. He left in late 2021, became a tenured (Huiyan Chair) professor in Tsinghua University's Department of Electronic Engineering in 2022, and founded the startup Frontis.ai (衔远科技).

In 2024, after the death of founding director Tang Xiao'ou, he became Director and Chief Scientist of the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, debuting at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in July 2024. His research spans AGI, large language models, AI safety and alignment and AI for science, with more than 200 papers. He is an IEEE Fellow and CAAI Fellow, has received the Wu Wenjun Award for Outstanding Contribution to AI, sits on China's National New Generation AI Governance Committee and is chief scientist of a national 'New Generation AI' megaproject.

zhou-bowen.views: Zhou argues that 'AI technology development must balance growth and safety'. At WAIC 2024 he proposed the 'AI-45° Law': in the long run AI safety and capability should advance together along a roughly 45-degree line, with 'safety and trustworthiness' built into AI's DNA as a core design principle rather than added afterwards. He has warned that current AI advances mostly on capability while safety lags behind. No numeric AGI timeline or p(doom) estimate was found.
